documents: The study screened for suitable ionizable cationic lipids and optimized the concentration of the synthetic lipid DMG-PEG 2000 to enhance RNP stability and delivery efficiency.
Adenine base editor and prime editor RNPs were encapsulated within lipid nanoparticles using the ionizable lipid SM102 via microfluidic mixing.
Cell-penetrating peptides were used either covalently fused to the protein or as excipients to enhance the efficiency of ribonucleoprotein delivery.

The CRISPR/Cas9 system utilized in gene editing trials consists of a Cas9 nuclease targeted to a genomic site by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and a guide RNA that focuses the binding of Cas9 on a 20-bp-long DNA protospacer.

Base and prime editors are designed by fusing a DNA effector domain to a partially inactivated Cas9 domain, termed a Cas9 nickase, to avoid non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and cytotoxicity caused by double-stranded DNA breaks.

The current standard for delivery of gene therapy and gene editing constructs is via viral vectors, specifically lentiviruses (LV) and adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), although base and prime editors delivered by AAV often require splitting into two viral vectors due to packaging limits.

Transient delivery mechanisms for CRISPR/Cas9 include virus-like particle (VLP) delivery, mRNA lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, and direct ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery as naked RNP or as a lipoplex with cationic lipid reagents such as Lipofectamine 2000.

The study utilized purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) for delivery, following a screening of cell-penetrating peptides and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid dissociation constants (pKa) greater than 6.
Protein purification was performed using Ni-NTA, size exclusion chromatography (SEC), TALON chromatography, and 1D4 chromatography, with purity verified by SDS-PAGE and western blot analysis.
The removal of contaminating nucleic acids during ABE purification was monitored by tracking the decrease in absorbance at 260 nm relative to 280 nm.
Size exclusion chromatography standards included blue dextran (2,000 kDa), thyroglobulin (670 kDa), γ-globulin (158 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and vitamin B12 (1.35 kDa).

Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) profiles for ABE were averaged from three replicates (n=3) in PBS containing 10% (w/v) sucrose, while DSF profiles for PE were averaged from three replicates (n=3) in PBS.

In vitro activity assays for ABE and PE were visualized using urea-PAGE gels imaged for fluorescein and SYBR Gold, with PE assays including controls for no substrate, substrate-only, no epegRNA, and no dNTP.

Cre recombinase was purified through nickel metal-affinity chromatography (Ni-NTA) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC), with purity confirmed by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) visualized with Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB) and anti-Cre western blot.

ABE8e was purified through affinity chromatography on TALON metal and 1D4 affinity columns, followed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), and its purity was assessed by SDS-PAGE with CBB staining and anti-Cas9 western blot.
PE2 was purified using a method similar to ABE8e, with an additional heparin chromatography step performed after 1D4 immunoaffinity to maximize separation from impurities.
The stability of ABE8e RNP and PE2 RNP was determined by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), and the ABE RNP was further stabilized by 10% (w/v) sucrose.
The enzymatic activity of ABE8e RNP was assessed by an in vitro deamination assay, and the enzymatic activity of PE2 RNP was assessed by an in vitro reverse-transcriptase extension assay.

Intracellular delivery of Cre recombinase was assessed in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cultured cell line, which expresses green fluorescent protein (GFP) constitutively and allows red fluorescent protein (RFP) expression upon Cre-mediated excision of a stop codon.
Cre recombinase was delivered as a lipoplex with Lipofectamine 3000 as a positive control to confirm the specificity of the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line.
In vivo activity was evaluated by injecting Cre recombinase subretinally into ROSA mT/mG mice, where tdTomato to eGFP conversion was detected by two-photon excitation.

The study utilized a color-switch Cre-reporter cell line where GFP is constitutively expressed and RFP is expressed only after Cre-mediated excision of the GFP gene and stop codon, with conversion quantified by flow cytometry using three biological replicates and two analytical replicates each.

Cre-mediated tdTomato to eGFP expression in the ROSA mT/mG Cre-reporter mouse model was measured one week after subretinal delivery using two-photon excitation microscopy, with the RPE layer oriented towards the top of the retinal cross-section.

For in vitro screening, NIH/3T3 cells were retrovirally transduced with a construct containing a fragment of Rpe65 rd12 cDNA with an in-frame nonsense mutation flanked by mCherry and eGFP, where unedited cells express only mCherry and successful editing results in mCherry-eGFP fusion protein expression.

Adenine base editing efficiency in the rd12 reporter cells was quantified by next-generation sequencing, which showed 22% editing, and by flow cytometry, which showed 32% conversion, following plasmid transfection of ABE8e with a previously validated rd12 sgRNA.
The addition of 10% w/v sucrose to the RNP mixture boosted delivery of the ABE8e RNP, and this effect was further enhanced 1.5-fold by the addition of the non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide.

Prime editing activity was not observed in the rd12 reporter cells when PE was delivered with 2% sucrose, but activity was noted when delivered with 10% sucrose, with the 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide improving PE2 RNP delivery efficiency by approximately 1.6-fold.
Genomic DNA and transcripts were sequenced from retinal pigment epithelium samples isolated from treated mice to quantify on-target genomic editing and base editing in cDNA.
The study utilized subretinal injection of ABE8e RNP into rd12 mice, with efficacy measured by the scotopic dark-adapted flash electroretinography b-wave.

ABE RNP was delivered in vitro to rd12 reporter cells using Lipofectamine 3000 at a concentration of 20 nM (4.5 μg ml⁻¹), and next-generation sequencing was used to analyze editing efficiency and precision.
The optimal in vitro formulation for ABE8e RNP delivery used 50 pmol (11.2 μg) of RNP per μl of Lipofectamine 3000, corresponding to a dose of 5.6 μg RNP per eye in vivo.

In vivo delivery utilized a Lipofectamine 3000 formulation at 50% by volume (0.5 μl per eye), which was compared against a 5-fold lower dose of Lipofectamine 3000 with the same amount of ABE RNP to assess toxicity.

The study utilized rd12 mice for in vivo testing of ABE RNP delivery via subretinal injection, with the LNP formulation containing 2.5% 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (SOPS) and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000.

The ABE RNP was delivered at a concentration of 2 μM (0.45 mg ml⁻¹, 450 ng per eye), which was at least 10-fold lower than the 20–36 μM (4.5–8.1 mg ml⁻¹, 4.5–8.1 μg per eye) concentrations used for RNPs formulated with sucrose or Lipofectamine 3000.
LNP stability was maintained for at least 28 days at -80 °C and at least 14 days at 4 °C, with the optimal lipid:RNA weight ratio determined to be at least 40:1.

Encapsulation efficiency was verified using a 1D4 immunoassay and size exclusion chromatography (SEC), while particle structure was characterized by cryoelectron microscopy (cryoEM) showing an approximate diameter of 100 nm.

Absolute quantification of ABE within the LNPs was performed through targeted proteomics, which detected Cas9 and TadA* deaminase peptides at the same level to confirm intact full-length ABE8e protein.

Editing outcomes were assessed via next-generation sequencing, which revealed up to 40% on-target editing and minimal off-target activity with ≤0.3% edited alleles at off-target sites in the rd12 cDNA cell line.
PE2 RNP delivery was tested at 500 nM (149 μg ml⁻¹) for PE compared with 20–100 nM (4.5–22.4 μg ml⁻¹) for ABE, with encapsulation verified by 1D4 immunoprecipitation assay and cryoEM.

Proteomic analysis of PE2 RNP LNPs showed that Cas9 and the reverse transcriptase (MMLVRT) were not detected at equimolar concentrations, indicating potential issues with LNP formulation or PE2 purification.

Next-generation sequencing of cells treated with PE RNP LNP confirmed exceptional purity of editing outcomes with no unwanted editing or off-target editing detected in the Rpe65 rd12 cDNA-bearing cells.

The study utilized a prototypical lipid mixture for LNP formulation consisting of ionizable lipid, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol, and 1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000 (DMG-PEG 2000) at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5.

To prevent ABE inactivation, the researchers selected ionizable lipids with pKa values above 6.0, specifically SM102 (pKa 6.68), CL4H6 (pKa 6.25), and DODMA (pKa 6.59), to facilitate protonation at the formulation pH of 6.0.
The hydrodynamic diameter of the resulting LNPs was measured between 200 and 250 nm using dynamic light scattering.

Encapsulation of ABE RNP within LNPs was verified by immunoprecipitation with 1D4 resin followed by anti-Cas9 western blot analysis, which distinguished encapsulated RNPs from free ABE RNPs in the non-bound fraction.
The ABE RNP LNPs were tested on rd12 reporter cells, where SM102 LNPs achieved nearly 100% conversion efficiency at a concentration of 20 nM ABE RNP (4.5 μg ml−1).
The lipoplex control using Lipofectamine 3000 peaked at approximately 50% cell conversion, representing a lower efficiency compared to the SM102 LNPs.

The rd12 reporter system consists of a gene under the CMV promoter expressing mCherry and eGFP with an intervening Rpe65 rd12 genomic sequence, where the c.130 C > T mutation prevents eGFP expression until base editing restores the reading frame.
Base editing efficiency in rd12 reporter cells was quantified 48 hours after co-transfection of CMV-ABE8e-NG and sgRNA plasmids, using three biological replicates with two analytical replicates each.
Delivery efficiency was assessed via fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry 48 hours post-treatment, with mCherry and eGFP co-expression indicating successful delivery.

Concentration dependence of ABE delivery was evaluated in the presence of 2% (w/v) sucrose, 10% (w/v) sucrose, or 0.5 μM ABE with 10% (w/v) sucrose and 6× His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, where 1 μM corresponds to 224 μg ml−1.
In vivo assessment utilized ERG response curves from rd12 mice two weeks post-treatment with ABE RNP in the presence of high and low NaCl and sucrose, with and without 6× His-CM18-PTD4 peptide.

The ABE RNP LNPs were formulated with ionizable lipids SM102, CL4H6, or DODMA and 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000, yielding diameters of 228 nm (PdI 0.072), 235 nm (PdI 0.132), and 249 nm (PdI 0.079) respectively, as measured by size-distribution analysis across 3 replicates.

In vitro delivery of ABE RNP to rd12 reporter cells was quantified by flow cytometry using an ABE RNP concentration of 20 nM (4.5 µg ml⁻¹) after incubation periods of 1-48 hours, with results reported as mean ± s.d. from two biological replicates with two analytical replicates each.

In vivo ERG b-wave responses in rd12 mice were assessed after subretinal injection of 1 µl ABE RNP LNP per eye, with ABE RNP concentrations of ~2.3 µM (515 ng per eye) for SM102/CL4H6 LNPs and ~1.8 µM (403 ng per eye) for DODMA LNPs, analyzed using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons test on at least 10 eyes.

The concentration of ABE RNP in the LNPs was estimated by correcting for dilution throughout encapsulation and dialysis, and verified by mass spectrometry targeting Cas9 and evolved adenosine deaminase TadA* peptides relative to absorbance at 280 nm across three analytical replicates.

Rescue of RPE65 expression in cells expressing Rpe65 rd12 cDNA was evaluated using ABE delivered via Lipofectamine 3000 or LNPs containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 1.5-2.5% DMG-PEG 2000, with editing outcomes analyzed by next-generation sequencing across three analytical replicates.

In vivo ERG b-wave responses in rd12 mice treated with 1 µl ABE RNP LNP per eye containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 1.5 or 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 were measured at RNP concentrations of ~2.3 and 2.5 µM (doses of 515 ng and 560 ng RNP per eye), with statistical analysis performed using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons test on at least 8 eyes.

The residence time of ABE in the mouse eye was determined by subretinal injection of optimized ABE RNP LNP with SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 into wild-type mice, followed by euthanasia at sequential intervals to assess ABE degradation kinetics in the neural retina and RPE.

Optimized ABE RNP LNP was delivered via subretinal injection into 3-4-week-old juvenile rd12 mice, with precise correction of Rpe65 genomic DNA and transcripts assessed two weeks post-injection, and retinoid levels assayed in whole eyes analyzed to detect 11-cis-retinal production.

The particle-size distribution of PE2 RNP LNP was analyzed for formulations prepared with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipids SM102, CL4H6, or DODMA, as well as with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipid SM102, using n = 3 replicates.

Delivery of PE2 RNP LNP to rd12 reporter cells was analyzed by flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy, with the representative microscopic image showing rd12 reporter cells treated with 20 nM (6 μg ml⁻¹) PE2 RNP LNP containing 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000.

The cryoelectron-microscopy imaging of PE2 RNP LNP containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 was performed using two biological replicates with two analytical replicates each, reporting mean ± s.d.

The study utilized LNP delivery systems where the lipid content exceeded the weight of the ribonucleoprotein complex by approximately eight times, a parameter that poses translational challenges in non-human primates or humans. The researchers noted that smaller LNPs, typically below 100 nm in diameter, are more readily internalized by cells, a characteristic relevant to the tight junctions and phagocytic role of the RPE.

The study evaluated functional outcomes in rd12 mice using ERG recordings, which demonstrated a noteworthy restoration of retinal function despite the observed editing efficiency of Rpe65 being lower than previously reported. The researchers identified that additional experiments are needed to correlate functional Rpe65 mRNA levels with the zygosity of corrected alleles of Rpe65 in rd12 mice.

The study referenced a previous investigation characterizing a RPE65-P2A-CreERT2 knock-in mouse model, where homozygous knock-in mice expressed RPE65 at levels amounting to only 1-5% of their wild-type counterparts yet exhibited ERG responses nearly indistinguishable from wild-type mice. The current study observed that editing resulted in the partial restoration of vision-dependent outcomes, specifically the pupillary light reflex and V1 and SC responses.

The study utilized a PE2 editing strategy without the introduction of a second guide RNA that programmes a nick on the unedited strand, which is distinct from the PE3 strategy that generally increases prime editing efficiency.

The researchers used anti-Cas9 western blot analysis of RPE/choroid/sclera and neural retina lysates collected at indicated hours post-injection to assess ABE RNP LNP degradation kinetics in wild-type mice.
The study employed next-generation sequencing of genomic DNA and transcripts to document Rpe65-editing outcomes after treatment with ABE RNP LNP or PE RNP LNP.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used to quantify 11-cisretinal in whole eyes from dark-adapted untreated rd12 mice, ABE-RNP-LNP- and PE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12 mice, and wild-type mice.
RPE flatmounts from rd12 untreated, ABE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12, and wild-type mice were stained for RPE65 (green) and counterstained with ZO-1 (magenta) and DAPI (blue).
Scotopic flash ERG a-wave and b-wave amplitudes were measured for rd12 mice to assess functional outcomes.
Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4(ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (JAX 007676) and crossed with other lines.

Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4(ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice (JAX 007676) were crossed with BALB/cJ albino mice (JAX 000651) to establish an albino ROSA mT/mG line, while C57BL/6J (JAX 000664) and rd12 (JAX 005379) mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and housed at the University of California, Irvine on a 12 h/12 h light/dark cycle.

The antennapedia (ANTP) DNA sequence was generated by annealing ANTP-Or_F and ANTP-Or_R oligonucleotides at a 1:1 molar ratio to a total DNA concentration of 80 μM in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 62.5 mM NaCl, and 10 mM EDTA, using a thermocycler protocol of 2 minutes at 95 °C followed by gradual cooling to 25 °C over 45 minutes.

Recombinant plasmids for N-terminal Cre recombinase fusion proteins were propagated in Escherichia coli NEB-5α cells (New England Biolabs, C2987H), with the pANTP-Cre plasmid constructed by replacing the TAT sequence with ANTP between Ncol and Ndel cloning sites.

A positive control Cre eVLP was produced by subcloning Cre (Addgene, 123133) into pCMV-MMLVgag-3xNES-ABE7.10-NG (Addgene, 181753) via USER cloning (NEB), and eVLPs were prepared following previously described methods.

Genes encoding ABE7.10, ABE8e, and PE2 constructs were subcloned into pRha rhamnose-inducible expression vectors via USER cloning (NEB), and the 1D4 peptide with a preceding tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition site was introduced by PCR site-directed mutagenesis and KLD cloning (NEB, M0554S).

Cell-penetrating peptide sequences were introduced into ABE using PAGE-purified single-strand oligonucleotides (Sigma-Aldrich) annealed at a final concentration of 25 μM in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 5 mM MgCl2 by heating at 95 °C for 5 minutes and slow cooling.

Assembled duplexes were ligated at a 100-fold excess into protein expression vectors linearized with FastDigest Ndel (Thermo Fisher, FD0584), transformed into NEB-5α cells, and plated onto LB-agar plates containing 25 μg ml-1 kanamycin, with candidate clones identified by colony PCR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing (GeneWiz).

Cre recombinase expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21star (DE3) (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown in Terrific Broth (TB; Thermo Fisher, 22711-022) with 50 µg ml⁻¹ kanamycin (Goldbio, K-120-SL25) overnight at 37 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m.

Cre recombinase production cultures were induced with 0.5 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG; Goldbio, I2481C25) when the absorbance at 600 nm reached 0.5, followed by incubation at 20 °C for 16 h.
Cre recombinase cells were collected by centrifugation at 7,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min, and the resulting pellets were stored at -80 °C.

Cre recombinase cell pellets from a 1.5-litre culture were resuspended in Cre-lysis buffer (50 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 1 M NaCl, 1 cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail tablet (MilliporeSigma, COEDTAF-RO) per 50 ml buffer) and lysed by sonication (125-W pulses, 5 s on/5 s off, for 10 min total) or French press (3 passes at up to 15,000 psi).
The Cre recombinase lysate was centrifuged at 48,500 g for 15 min and incubated with 1 ml of Ni-Sepharose High Performance beads (Cytiva, 17526801) in a rotating mixer for 1 h.

The Ni-Sepharose resin was centrifuged at 500 g for 5 min, washed with 40 ml of Cre-wash buffer (25 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl), and packed in a Tricorn 5/50 column connected to a Bio-Rad DuoFlow system (Bio-Rad) for perfusion at 0.5 ml min⁻¹.

Cre recombinase proteins were eluted with 30 ml of a continuous gradient of Cre-elution buffer (25 mM Na phosphate, pH 7.4, containing 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole) after washing the resin with 20 ml of Cre-wash buffer or until a stable absorbance baseline was observed.

Fractions containing Cre recombinase were identified by SDS-PAGE and CBB staining (Quick Coomassie stain, Anatrace, GEN-QC-STAIN-1L), concentrated, and subjected to size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 28990944) or a HiLoad 16/600 Superdex 200 pg column (28989335) using P500G buffer (20 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol) as the mobile phase.
Pure Cre recombinase fractions were concentrated, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 °C.
ABE and PE expression plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown overnight on Luria-Bertani (LB)-agar plates with 25 µg ml⁻¹ kanamycin.
One and a half litre of TB with kanamycin was inoculated with 10 ml of starter culture and grown at 37 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m. until the cells reached an A₆₀₀ₙₘ of 1.5.

ABE and PE protein expression was induced with 0.8% (w/v) rhamnose (Goldbio, R-105-250) after cooling the cultures in an ice-water slurry for 30 min to 1 h, and the proteins were expressed at 17 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m. for 16-24 h.
ABE and PE cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the pellets were stored at -80 °C.
Proteins were expressed at 17 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m. for 16-24 h, and the resulting cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C.

Thawed cells from a 1.5-L culture were homogenized with a 40 ml Dounce homogenizer in lysis buffer containing 100 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH 8.0), 1 M NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 5 mM TCEP, and 1 cOmplete Ultra EDTA-Free protease inhibitor tablet per 40 ml.
Cell lysis was achieved by sonication with a Qsonica Q125 sonicator (125 W) using a 1/8-inch microtip at 100% amplitude for a total of 20 min with intermittent pulses of 5 s on and 5 s off.
The lysate was clarified at 4 °C by centrifugation at 48,500 g for 10 min, and ABE was captured on a 3-ml TALON metal-affinity resin (Takara Bio, 635502).

The TALON resin was washed with 100 ml of lysis buffer without inhibitors and 10 ml of wash buffer containing 100 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH 8.0), 500 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, and 1 mM TCEP, before elution with wash buffer supplemented with 150 mM imidazole.

ABE was further purified by immunoaffinity chromatography using a 4 ml 1D4 resin (Sepharose CL-4B; Cytiva, 17043001) packed in a DWK Life Sciences Kimble Kontes FlexColumn, immobilizing 5-10 mg ml⁻¹ of in-house purified 1D4 antibody.
The 1D4 column was washed with at least 40 ml of wash buffer at 0.5 ml min⁻¹, and ABE was eluted with 1 mg ml⁻¹ 1D4 peptide in wash buffer at approximately 1 ml h⁻¹.

Pooled ABE fractions were purified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column or a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column, eluted with storage buffer containing 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, and 20% glycerol.

Pure ABE was concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters with 30-kDa molecular weight cut-off membranes (Merck, UFC903024), sterilized through 0.22-μm filters, quantified by UV absorption at 280 nm, and snap frozen at -80 °C.
PE cells were lysed using a single pass through a French press followed by sonication for 10 min, and subsequent metal affinity and immunoaffinity steps used a wash buffer containing 400 mM NaCl.
PE was subjected to heparin-affinity chromatography on a HiTrap Heparin HP 5 ml column (Cytiva, 17040703) at 0.5 ml min⁻¹, equilibrated with wash buffer containing 400 mM NaCl.
The heparin column was washed with at least 50 ml of wash buffer until the UV baseline stabilized, and bound proteins were eluted with a 200-ml NaCl gradient ranging from 0.4 M to 1.0 M.

Selected PE fractions were purified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column with storage buffer containing 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, and 5% (v/v) glycerol, then concentrated, filtered, quantified at 280 nm, and snap frozen at -80 °C.

Protein purity was assessed using SDS-PAGE in hand-cast Tris-glycine-SDS discontinuous gels with 4% acrylamide in a stacking gel (pH 6.8) and 10% acrylamide in a resolving gel (pH 8.8) with 2.7% crosslinker (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio of 37.5:1; Bio-Rad, 1610158). Samples were mixed with 4x-concentrated Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610747) and supplemented with 50 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; MilliporeSigma, D9779), denatured at 70 °C for 10 min, and centrifuged before application to the gel.

Protein concentration was quantified using UV absorption spectroscopy by measuring absorbance at 280 nm with a Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer, and contaminating nucleic acids were monitored by the ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 280 nm, where a ratio <0.60 indicated protein free from nucleic acids.
Extinction coefficients of the protein constructs were estimated using the ProtParam tool available at https://web.expasy.org/protparam/.

Synthetic 60-bp-long DNA oligonucleotides (Sigma) labelled with fluorescein on the strand undergoing deamination were annealed at a 1:1 ratio in 10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA by incubation at 95 °C for 5 min and subsequent slow cooling to 20 °C.

End-modified sgRNA and epegRNA were ordered from IDT Technologies, featuring 2'-O-methyl groups on the first three and last three nucleotides, with the first and last three phosphodiester bonds replaced by phosphorothioate bonds.
Guide RNAs were dissolved in nuclease-free water at 37 °C for 15 min at 500 r.p.m. in a thermomixer and folded by incubation at ~75 °C for 5 min, followed by slow cooling.

Prepared nucleic acids were quantified using UV absorption spectroscopy by measuring absorbance at 260 nm, where an A260 nm value of 1.0 corresponded to a DNA concentration of 50 μg ml−1 or an RNA concentration of 40 μg ml−1.
The study used HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells (CS cell line), NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, rd12 reporter cells, and primary fibroblasts isolated from P0-P3 ROSA mT/mG mice.

HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells, NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, and rd12 reporter cells were maintained in DMEM/F12 medium with GlutaMAX supplement or DMEM with glutamine, both supplemented with 10% FBS and optional 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO₂.

Primary fibroblasts were isolated from the skin of P0-P3 ROSA mT/mG mice by digesting skins with a 1:1 mixture of 0.25% trypsin without EDTA and 5 U ml⁻¹ dispase for 1 h at 37 °C, followed by digestion with 0.25% collagenase I in serum-free DMEM/F12 for 1 h at 37 °C.

Isolated primary fibroblasts were filtered through a 70-µm strainer, washed with DMEM/F12 containing 15% FBS and 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin via two centrifugation steps at 180 g for 5 min at room temperature, and passaged every 3-4 days using 0.05% trypsin-EDTA.

For protein delivery experiments, cells were seeded 24 h before the experiment in 24-, 48-, and 96-well plates to reach 50-70% confluency, with specific cell counts of 100,000, 50,000, and 25,000 cells per well for the CS cell line and NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, and 50,000, 24,000, and 10,000 cells per well for rd12 reporter cells and primary fibroblasts.
Two-photon imaging of enucleated mouse eyes used a Ti:sapphire laser (Coherent, Vision S) set to 950 nm, attenuated by an electro-optic modulator, with a 1.0 NA×20 Leica objective.
Spectral separation for the two-photon imaging was achieved using two internal detectors with bandwidths set to 490-545 nm for GFP and 590-680 nm for tdTomato.

The rd12 reporter cell line was generated by transducing NIH/3T3 cells with retrovirus from Phoenix-Eco cells transfected with pMXs-mCherry-rd12-eGFP-IRES-blasticidin, followed by selection with blasticidin (5 µg ml⁻¹) for 10 days.

Surviving rd12 reporter cells were sorted via flow cytometry for high-expressing mCherry-positive clones, seeded into 96-well plates, and screened for editability via co-transfection with pCMV-NG-SpCas9-ABE7.10max and pSPgRNA-rd12-A6.
No additional characterization was performed on the sorted rd12 reporter cells beyond sequencing.

ABE ribonucleoprotein was assembled by incubating ABE with a 1.5-fold molar excess of sgRNA in a reaction buffer containing 20 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH 7.5), 100 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgSO4, 2 mM DTT, and 5% (v/v) glycerol for 15 minutes at room temperature, with additional 10% (w/v) sucrose added when RNPs were assembled above 4 μM.

For the ABE enzymatic assay, ABE was diluted to 1 μM with the reaction buffer, preheated at 37 °C, and added with 15 ng of DNA substrate (0.02 μM final), with deamination conducted for 10–60 minutes for ABE8e.

The 20-μl ABE reactions were quenched by adding 30 μl of water preheated to 95 °C and incubating for 2 minutes at 95 °C, followed by treatment with 1 μl of RNase A (20 mg ml−1) and 1 μl of proteinase K (20 mg ml−1) for 15 minutes at room temperature.

Purified DNA from the ABE assay was nicked with 5 units of Endonuclease V (EndoV, NEB) for 2–3 hours at 37 °C, then quenched by adding TriTrack DNA-loading dye (1× final) and incubating at 95 °C for 2 minutes.

Cleavage products from the ABE assay were analyzed by denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis with urea (Urea-PAGE) in Bio-Rad MiniProtean continuous hand-cast 15% acrylamide gels in Tris-borate-EDTA (TBE) with 7 M urea and 5% crosslinker (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio of 19:1), maintaining at least 42 °C in the electrophoresis chamber.

Imaging for the ABE assay was performed using the ChemiDoc MP system (Bio-Rad), with fluorescein detection done immediately after electrophoresis and SYBR Gold (Thermo Fisher, S11494) detection done after 30 minutes of staining with 1× dye in 1×TBE.
The in vitro reverse-transcriptase elongation assay for PE was carried out in the same reaction buffer as for ABE, supplemented with 0.5 mM deoxyribonucleotides (dNTP).
PE2 RNP was assembled with a 1.1-fold molar excess of epegRNA targeting the rd12 locus in the reaction buffer without added sucrose for 15 minutes at room temperature.

In the PE assay, reactions were preheated at 37 °C and 45 ng of fluorescein-labelled substrate was added to a final volume of 15 μl, followed by quenching with 1 μl each of proteinase K (20 mg ml−1) and RNase A (20 mg ml−1) after 15 minutes.
The PE assay reaction was denatured at 95 °C for 2 minutes, supplemented with 6× TriTrack loading dye, and 15 ng of substrate was analyzed by Urea-PAGE using the same conditions as the ABE assay.

For differential scanning fluorimetry, ABE and PE proteins were complexed with a 1.5-fold molar excess of guide RNA in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at room temperature for 15 minutes to obtain 10 μM RNP, with ABE RNP containing an additional 10% (w/v) sucrose.

The RNPs for differential scanning fluorimetry were diluted with PBS to 1 μM, SYPRO Orange probe was added to a final concentration of 5×, and samples were aliquoted (10 μl per well) into a 384-well plate (Applied Biosystems, 4483319) sealed with optical foil (Applied Biosystems, 4360954).
After an additional 15 minutes of incubation, the 384-well plate was centrifuged at 1,000 g for 1 minute at room temperature and installed in a pre-equilibrated Bio-Rad CFX384 thermocycler.

Fluorescence for differential scanning fluorimetry was measured in Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) mode every 0.2 °C from 20 °C to 95 °C, with the rate of change of fluorescence (-dF/dT) used to estimate the melting temperature (Tm).
All differential scanning fluorimetry samples were run in triplicate, and plots of averaged data are reported.

Complementary DNA was synthesized from RNA using the High Capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Thermo Fisher, 4387406), and 0.5-1 μl of the isolated genomic DNA or cDNA was used as input for the first PCR reaction (PCR1). PCR1 amplified genomic loci using Phusion Plus polymerase (Thermo Fisher, F631S) with a thermal profile of 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 30 cycles at 98 °C for 10 s, 60 °C for 20 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, ending with 72 °C for 5 min.

One microlitre of the PCR1 product was used as input for PCR2 to install Illumina barcodes, which was conducted for 9 cycles of amplification using a Phusion HS II kit (Life Technologies). Following PCR2, samples were pooled and gel purified in a 1% agarose gel using a Qiaquick Gel Extraction kit (Qiagen), and library concentration was quantified using the Qubit High-Sensitivity Assay kit (Thermo Fisher).

Samples were sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq instrument using an Illumina MiSeq 300 v. 2 kit (Illumina) with paired-end reads, where read 1 was 200-280 cycles and read 2 was 0 cycles. Sequencing reads were demultiplexed using MiSeq Reporter software (Illumina) and analyzed using CRISPResso2 in batch analysis mode, with reads filtered by a minimum average quality score of Q>30.

The CRISPResso2 analysis used quantification window parameters of -w 20 and -wc-10. Base editing efficiencies were reported as the percentage of sequencing reads containing a given base conversion at a specific position, and Prism 10 (GraphPad) was used to generate dot plots and bar plots.

ABE RNP was assembled by incubating up to 20 μM ABE with a 1.1-fold excess of sgRNA in OptiMEM medium supplemented with 10% (w/v) sucrose for at least 15 minutes at room temperature. The sgRNA used contained additional modifications and was supplied by IDT.

The 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide was dissolved in 100 mM HEPES pH 8.0 to achieve a concentration of 10 mM, resulting in a final stock solution pH of approximately 7.0. This peptide stock was diluted to 400 μM with water, added to the ABE RNP, and incubated for an additional 15 minutes.

CPP fusions of ABE with or without the 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide were diluted to final concentrations in OptiMEM containing 2% or 10% sucrose. 100 μl of each mixture was applied to cells in a 48-well plate washed with OptiMEM medium, and the medium was exchanged with 250 μl of complete medium after 3 hours.

Lipofectamine 3000 lipoplexes were assembled by diluting 0.5 μl of Lipofectamine 3000 per well in a 48-well plate or 0.2 μl per well in a 96-well plate with OptiMEM containing 10% (w/v) sucrose to volumes of 12.5 μl and 5 μl, respectively. ABE RNPs diluted with OptiMEM containing 10% (w/v) sucrose to 12.5 μl (48-well) or 5 μl (96-well) were added to the diluted lipids and incubated for 15 minutes at room temperature.

A 25 μl lipoplex of ABE with Lipofectamine 3000 was added to cells with 225 μl fresh complete medium in a 48-well plate, or 10 μl was added with 90 μl medium in a 96-well plate. The cells were incubated for 48 hours before analysis.

Plasmid DNA transfections were performed in 48-well plates using 160 ng pCMV-NG-SpCas9-ABE, 80 ng pSPgRNA-rd12-A6, and 0.75 μl Lipofectamine 3000 per well following the manufacturer protocol. PE was delivered in vitro similarly to ABE but without sucrose, unless otherwise noted.

Activities of ABE and PE in the rd12 reporter cell line were analyzed by fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry. Rescue of RPE65 expression was analyzed using NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing Rpe65 rd12 cDNA, which were treated with ABE and PE and detached with trypsin after 48 hours.

One-tenth of the cell suspension from NIH/3T3 cells was lysed with 10 mM Tris pH 7.5 and 0.05% SDS containing 0.02 mg ml⁻¹ proteinase K for 1 hour at 37°C, followed by proteinase K inactivation at 85°C for 45 minutes. Remaining NIH/3T3 cells were lysed in 1× RIPA buffer (Cell Signaling Technology, 9806) with 1× cOmplete Ultra EDTA-free protease inhibitors (Roche) for 1 hour on a rotator in a cold room. The lysate was centrifuged at 17,000–21,400 g for 20 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was used for analysis.
Protein concentration in the extracts from NIH/3T3 cells was measured using the BCA assay (Thermo Fisher, 23252). The extracts were then subjected to western blotting.
Mouse eyes were enucleated and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at room temperature, followed by three 5-minute washes in PBS.
RPE flatmounts were created by removing the anterior segment and retina from the posterior eyecup and making four radial cuts towards the optic nerve to flatten the eyecup.
Samples were permeabilized and blocked in 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, T8532) with 3% normal goat serum in PBS for 30 min.

Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C with mouse anti-RPE65 antibody (1:100; in house) and rabbit anti-ZO-1 polyclonal antibody (1:100; Invitrogen, 61-7300) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100, and 3% normal goat serum.

After three 5-minute washes in PBS, samples were incubated for 2 hours at room temperature in the dark with Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher, A11032) and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100, and 3% normal goat serum.

Flatmounts were incubated in DAPI (1 μg ml⁻¹; Thermo Fisher, 62248) in PBS for 10 min, washed three times in PBS for 5 min each, and mounted with VECTASHIELD HardSet Antifade Mounting Medium (Vector Labs, H-1400-10).
Immunohistochemistry samples were imaged on a Keyence BZ-X810 All-in-One fluorescence microscope.
Supernatant was pre-cleared with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Fisher, 10003D) by rotation at 4 °C for 15 min to remove immunoglobulin contaminants from blood before loading on the gel.

Western blotting utilized mouse anti-RPE65 antibody (produced in house) or mouse anti-SpCas9 (clone 7A9, Biolegend, 844302) diluted 1:1,000 in 5% non-fat dry milk in PBS (Bio-Rad, 1610780) with 0.1% Tween 20 (MilliporeSigma, P9416).

The western blot membranes were incubated with primary antibodies overnight in the cold room, washed four times with PBST for 5 minutes each, and incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-linked horse anti-mouse antibody (Vector Laboratories, PI-2000-1) diluted 1:2,500 in 5% non-fat dry milk in PBST.

After stripping, western blot membranes were re-probed for 1 hour at room temperature with rabbit anti-β-actin polyclonal antibody (1:2,000; Cell Signaling Technology, 4970S) and developed using goat anti-rabbit IgG with HRP (1:2,500; Cell Signaling Technology, 7074S).
ABE was diluted into OptiMEM containing 10 or 25% (w/v) sucrose or into ABE storage buffer with 390 mM NaCl final concentration without added sucrose.

Samples were mounted with VECTASHIELD HardSet Antifade Mounting Medium (Vector Labs, H-1400-10) and imaged on a Keyence BZ-X810 All-in-One fluorescence microscope.
Mice were dark adapted for 1 week and anaesthetized by isoflurane inhalation before electroretinography (ERG) recording.

Pupils were dilated with topical 1% tropicamide ophthalmic solution (Akorn, 17478-102-12) and 10% phenylephrine ophthalmic solution (MWI Animal Health, 054243), followed by hypromellose (Akorn, 9050-1) for hydration.

Mice were placed on a heated Diagnosys Celeris rodent-ERG device with ocular stimulator electrodes on the corneas, a reference electrode subdermally between the ears, and a ground electrode in the rear leg.
Eyes were stimulated with a green-light flash stimulus (peak emission 544 nm, bandwidth ~160 nm) of -0.3 log (cd s m^-2) light intensity.
The responses for 10 stimuli with an inter-stimulus interval of 10 s were averaged to acquire a- and b-wave amplitudes from the ERG waveform.
Electroretinography data were analysed with the Espion V6 software (Diagnosys).
In the RNP LNP optimization study, eyes that received LNP and had no ERG response after treatment were excluded from the analyses.
The pupillary light reflex (PLR) was characterized in mice (n=5 for each group) using the A2000 computerized pupillometer (Neuroptics).
Mice were dark adapted for 6 h before PLR recordings in a dark room.
The A2000 pupillometer system uses two infrared cameras to independently record and track the dynamics of each pupil.
The light profile for PLR testing consisted of four white-light stimuli (1.2 log, 10^1.2 W m^-2), each lasting 500 ms.
Mice were kept under isoflurane anaesthesia during the PLR testing routine, which was carried out under scotopic conditions with no background illumination from the pupillometer.

The maximum size of the pupil after dark adaptation was quantified at 2 min after anaesthesia to establish baseline size, and pupil response was expressed as percent constriction compared to this baseline.
Digital movies of pupil responses were recorded using Active Presenter software (v.9.1.3, Atomi Systems).
Recorded videos were decomposed into individual frames using Adobe Premiere Rush programme (v.10.0.1, Adobe Systems) for manual verification and calculation of absolute pupil diameters.

Individual frames were processed using the Adobe Premiere Rush programme (v.10.0.1, Adobe Systems) for manual verification of pupil dynamics and calculation of absolute pupil diameters from the recorded images.

Mice were dark adapted for 2 days before eye enucleation, and eyes were homogenized in 1 ml of a 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) containing 50% (v/v) methanol (Sigma-Aldrich, 34860-1L-R) and 100 mM hydroxylamine (pH 8.0) (Sigma-Aldrich, 159417-100G).
After a 15 min incubation at room temperature, 2 ml of 3 M NaCl was added to the homogenized eye samples, which were then extracted twice with 3 ml ethyl acetate (Fisher Scientific, E195-4).

The combined organic phase was dried in vacuo and reconstituted in 250 μl hexane, after which 100 μl of the extracted retinoids were separated on a normal-phase HPLC column (Zorbax Sil, 5 μm, 4.6 mm × 250 mm; Agilent Technologies) connected to an Agilent Infinity 1260 HPLC system equipped with a diode-array detector.

Separation was achieved with a mobile phase of 0.6% ethyl acetate in hexane (Fisher Scientific, H302-4) at a flow rate of 1.4 ml min⁻¹ for 17 min, followed by a step increase to 10% ethyl acetate in hexane for an additional 25 min.
Retinoids were detected by monitoring absorbances at 325 nm and 360 nm using Agilent ChemStation software.
RNPs were assembled by mixing 10 μM purified ABE or PE with synthetic sgRNA (ABE) or epegRNA (PE) at a 1:1.1 molar ratio.
The buffer for ABE was 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol; for PE, the buffer was 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, 5% (v/v) glycerol; and guide RNA was dissolved in water.
Proteins were diluted, supplemented with 10% (w/v) sucrose from 50% (w/v) stock in water and added to guide RNA.
The final composition of the buffer in which RNPs were assembled was 2.8 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 140 mM NaCl, 10% (w/v) sucrose, 5.6% (v/v) glycerol for ABE; or 1.4% (v/v) glycerol for PE.
The RNPs were incubated at room temperature for at least 15 min.
Immediately before encapsulation, RNPs were diluted to 0.711 μM in a 50 mM Tris-acetate buffer (pH 6.0) with 10% (w/v) sucrose to achieve a final NaCl concentration of 10 mM.

The lipids used to encapsulate pre-formed RNPs comprised an ionizable cationic lipid (either CL4H6 (Cayman Chemical, 37279), SM102 (Broadpharm, BP-25499) or DODMA (Avanti Polar Lipids, 890899), all of which have pKas > 6.0 at 6.25, 6.68 and 6.59, respectively) and co-lipids DSPC (Avanti Polar Lipids, 850365), cholesterol (Avanti Polar Lipids, 700100) and DMG-PEG 2000 (Avanti Polar Lipids, 880151) at a molar composition of 50/10/38.5/1.5, respectively.
For optimization of DMG-PEG 2000 lipid content from 1.5 to 10 mole%, the concentration of cholesterol was decreased accordingly.
In some formulations, 2.5 mole% of SOPS (18:0-18:1 PS, Avanti Polar Lipids, 840039C) was used with 7.5 mole% of DSPC.

The lipids were dissolved in ethanol and rapidly combined with pre-formed RNP at a volume ratio of 1:3 (ethanol:aqueous) and a total lipid:guide RNA weight ratio of 40:1 (approximate total lipid:protein weight ratio of 7.75:1).

The study's reproducibility is compromised by the omission of specific software versions and library dependencies from the GitHub README, which prevents independent verification that the numerical outputs in Table 2 are not artifacts of specific library updates.

Verification of the two surviving outcomes is blocked by the missing exact random seed and package versions, making it impossible to confirm whether the FDR threshold was applied correctly in the code environment used to generate the corrected p-values.

The statistical robustness of the two surviving effects is undermined by the lack of reported effect sizes and confidence interval widths, particularly given the likely modest sample size and the strict Bonferroni threshold of 0.0042, which suggests the true magnitude of benefit is far less precise than the raw p < 0.05 values indicate.

The study utilized the huR83C humanized mouse model, which carries the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant, to evaluate the efficacy of the BEAM-301 formulation. BEAM-301 consists of lipid nanoparticles containing a newly engineered adenine base editor.
The researchers monitored phenotypic correction in the huR83C mice for a duration of one year following the administration of the BEAM-301 base editor.

The study utilized a newly created humanized knock-in G6PC1-R83C mouse strain (huR83C) generated by inserting the entire human G6PC1-R83C (G6PC1-c.247C > T) coding sequence into exon 1 of the mouse G6pc gene.
The huR83C mouse model was engineered to knock out native mouse G6pc gene expression while placing the expression of the human G6PC1-R83C under the control of the mouse G6pc promoter/enhancer.
The huR83C mice manifested a human GSD-Ia pathophysiology similar to global G6pc-deficient (G6pc-/-) mice, characterized by a lack of hepatic and renal G6Pase-α activity.

The study evaluated the efficacy of a newly-engineered adenine base editor (ABE) delivered via a single systemic administration of LNP-encapsulated mRNA (BEAM-301) at doses of 1.5 mg/kg (high) and 0.75 mg/kg (low) to newborn mice within 48 hours post-birth or at 3 weeks of age.

The experimental design utilized wild-type (mR83) mice with two functional mouse G6pcR83 alleles, homozygous (huR83C) mice with the human G6PC1-R83C variant knocked-in at the G6pc locus, and heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice, with the wild-type and heterozygous groups serving as controls.

Liver and kidney microsomal G6Pase-alpha activity was quantified in 3-week-old wild-type, heterozygous, and homozygous huR83C mice, establishing a lower level of quantitation of 2 units for the assay which confirmed the huR83C mice had null hepatic and renal G6pc loci.
The base editor used in the study harbors an saCas9 nickase domain and a TadA deaminase domain engineered to maximize editing of the target adenine and reduce editing of bystander adenines.
A guide RNA was designed with an saCas9 'NNGRRT' protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) to target the adenine at position 16 for the correction of the G6PC1-R83C variant.
The guide RNA and messenger RNA encoding the base-editor were co-formulated into a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) to generate the investigational therapy BEAM-301.
BEAM-301 was administered systemically via tail vein injection at doses of 0.1 to 3.0 mg/kg to 10-12-week-old heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice.
The base-editing efficiency of the G6PC1 alleles was analyzed via next-generation sequencing (NGS) in isolated liver slices at 7 days post-dose.
The functional impact of the non-synonymous Y85H edit was evaluated using transient expression assays in COS1 cells.
In heterozygous mice administered BEAM-301 at 1.5 mg/kg, an average of 40.3% of sequencing reads encoded wild-type G6Pase-α, while 5.5% contained the nonsynonymous Y85H bystander edit.

Primary human hepatocytes from 3 donors were treated with BEAM-301 at or near saturation of on-target editing. The rhAmpSeq method was used to amplify candidate off-target sites in parallel in treated and untreated (control, donor-matched) cells, followed by NGS processing to assess enriched editing in treated versus untreated cells.

Newborn huR83C mice were treated by systemic administration of BEAM-301 at a dose level of 1.5 mg/kg (301H), and metabolic correction was assessed at 3 weeks of age. Two of the eight treated mice were excluded from analysis because genomic analysis confirmed the absence of base-editing in their livers, suggesting failed administration of BEAM-301.
Histochemical enzyme analysis was performed on liver and kidney sections of heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) and edited huR83C mice to determine the distribution pattern of G6Pase-α activity.
Newborn huR83C mice were treated with a high dose of BEAM301 (301H) at 1.5 mg/kg while non-fasted, and the phenotype of the resulting NB-301H mice was evaluated at age 3 weeks.

The study compared NB-301H-3W mice to age-matched unedited huR83C (huR83C-3W), wild-type (mR83-3W), and heterozygote (mR83/huR83C-3W) mice, with sample sizes ranging from n=5 to n=25 depending on the specific assay.
Statistical analysis was performed using a two-tailed unpaired T test, with data presented as Mean values ± SEM and individual data points displayed for each animal.

Biochemical analysis at 3 weeks included measurements of blood glucose, serum cholesterol, serum triglyceride, serum lactate, uric acid, liver glucose, triglyceride, lactate, glycogen, and G6P levels, with sample sizes ranging from n=6 to n=24 across the control, huR83C-3W, and NB-301H-3W groups.

The study used 10-12-week-old heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice that were not fasted, treated via systemic administration of BEAM-301, with target site sequences analyzed one week later using next-generation sequencing (NGS).
Statistical analysis of the allele frequencies resulting from dosing heterozygous mice at 1.5 mg/kg (301H) was performed using a two-tailed unpaired T test, with data presented as Mean values ± SEM.
Validation of off-target sites was conducted in primary human hepatocytes using a 2-stage approach involving nomination and validation of candidate sites.

Potential off-target sites were nominated using two complementary biochemical assays: oligonucleotide enrichment and sequencing (ONE-seq) and Digenome-seq, which detects genome-wide base deamination and nicking events on naked genomic DNA.

A total of 591 unique candidate sites were selected for further evaluation in cells, including sites nominated from ONE-seq or Digenome-seq experiments, in silico identified low-mismatch sites, the on-target site, and 20 negative control sites.

Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on liver and kidney sections to assess tissue changes.

Oil Red O staining was used to confirm neutral fat accumulation in the liver and kidney of 3-week-old huR83C mice, showing increased hepatic fat with little or no renal fat accumulation.

ABE mRNA and gRNA targeting G6PC1-R83C were co-encapsulated at a 1:1 weight ratio in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) by rapidly mixing an acidic aqueous RNA solution with an ethanol solution containing a proprietary ionizable lipid, distearoylphosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and a lipid-anchored polyethylene glycol.

The LNP formulations were generated using a benchtop microfluidics device from Precision Nanosystems Inc., then dialyzed overnight at 4 °C against 1× Tris-buffered saline (pH 7.4) and concentrated using 100,000 Da molecular weight cutoff Amicon Ultra centrifugation tubes.
The total RNA concentration of the LNP formulations was determined using Quant-iT Ribogreen, and the particle size was determined using a Malvern Panalytical Zetasizer.

Frozen mouse liver tissues were homogenized in Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline using an Omni Prep Multi-Sample Homogenizer, and genomic DNA was isolated in duplicate using the MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Kit per the manufacturer's protocol.
Genomic DNA samples were eluted in MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Elution Solution, quantified using a Lunatic UV/Vis plate reader, and normalized to 20 ng/µl using the same elution solution.

The study utilized mR83, mR83/huR83C, and huR83C/huR83C mice in a mixed C57BL/6/129S4/SvJaeJ background, designated as C57BL-50/129-50, which was achieved through a specific mating strategy to ensure approximately 50% C57BL/6 and 50% 129S4/SvJaeJ ancestry.
To prevent inbreeding bias, the study protocol specified that progenies from the same litter or the same breeding cage were never mated together.

The ABE mRNA was produced by in vitro transcription from a template plasmid containing a T7 promoter, 5' UTR, base editor open reading frame, 3' UTR, and 120 polyA tail, using the NEB HiScribe T7 High-Yield RNA synthesis kit (E2040S) with CleanCap AG reagent (N-7113) and complete substitution of N1-methylpseudouridine triphosphate for uridine-5'-O-triphosphate.

Template plasmids for mRNA synthesis were prepared using ZymoPURE II plasmid kits (D4200), linearized by restriction digestion, purified by phenol-chloroform extraction, and the resulting transcripts were purified by lithium chloride precipitation.

Primary human hepatocytes (F00995-P) were seeded in CP medium (Z99029) onto collagen type I coated 24-well plates (356408) at a density of 350,000 cells/well and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2, with fibroblast cells (EF3003) added to generate hepatic co-cultures.

Lentiviral transduction was performed using ultra-purified recombinant lentivirus (Lot 220807LVB01) packaging a G6PC1 copy with the c.247C>T mutation at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 40 to introduce the target site into the hepatocyte cultures.

Cell transfection was performed using MessengerMAX transfection reagent (LMRNA015) co-formulated with base editor mRNA and gRNA at a 3:1 ratio, and cells were harvested for genomic DNA analysis at 7 days post-transfection.

Animal studies were conducted under protocols approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development or the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at University of Massachusetts Medical School and CRADL in Cambridge, Massachusetts, adhering to ARRIVE guidelines. Mice were maintained on a standard NIH-31 Open formula mouse/rat sterilizable diet (Envigo) or Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 diet (labdiet) without restrictions.

Mice were housed in a 12-hour light/dark cycle with ambient temperature controlled within 65-75 °F (18-24 °C) and humidity between 40-60%, and litter sizes were reduced to 6-8 pups to minimize feeding competition. Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide following the AVMA guidelines for the Euthanasia of Small Laboratory and Wild-Caught Rodents, 2020 Edition.

Potential off-target sites were identified using the Cas-OFFinder software tool on the GRCh38/hg38 human reference genome with a relaxed PAM requirement of NNGRRN and mismatch parameters allowing either 7 or fewer mismatches with no bulges, or a 2-base bulge with up to 3 mismatches.
The ONE-seq assay was performed on a SurePrint Oligonucleotide Library containing 14,509 sites using a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

Digenome-seq was performed using human genomic DNA isolated from the GM11468 human B-lymphocyte cell line, which is heterozygous for the G6PC1 c.247C > T allele, and a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

Multiplex amplicon sequencing via rhAmpSeq was performed on genomic DNA isolated from primary human hepatocytes treated with BEAM-301 at a concentration at or above the EC90 of on-target editing, with controls consisting of untreated, donor-matched primary human hepatocytes.

The EC90 for BEAM-301 was measured in primary human hepatocytes that harbor the target site introduced via lentiviral transduction to enable detection of the on-target edit, since healthy human hepatocytes do not harbor the target allele.
Sequencing reads were trimmed, stitched, aligned to the GRCh38/hg38 human genome reference sequence, and filtered for a minimum base-quality score of 30 and a mapping quality of 10.

Statistical significance for the enrichment of observed variants in treated samples relative to untreated samples was assessed using a Fisher's exact test based on an empirically determined threshold.
Genomic DNA samples were normalized to 20 ng/\u00b5l using MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Elution Solution.

Barcoded amplicons were generated in 25-\u00b5l PCR reactions using Q5 2× Hot Start Master Mix, 0.5 mM barcode primers, and 2 \u00b5l of the prior PCR reaction.
Barcoded amplicons were purified via DNA agarose gel extraction (D4008; Zymo Research Corporation) or SPRIselect bead cleanup (B23318; Beckman Coulter).
Final clean libraries were quantified using a Qubit 4 Fluorometer (Q33238; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq Instrument.

Targeted NGS data were analyzed by performing five steps: Illumina demultiplexing, read trimming and filtering, alignment of all reads to the expected amplicon sequence, generation of alignment statistics and quantification of base-edited alleles, and calculation of the frequencies of corrected G6PC1 alleles.
Primary human hepatocytes were harvested from 3 donor livers (BiolVT) and plated on BioCoat Rat Collagen I, 24-well plate (354408; Corning) according to manufacturer's instructions.
BEAM-301 was diluted in INVITROGRO CP media (Z990003; BioIVT) and added to the culture wells at the desired concentration.

BEAM-301-dosed huR83C mice did not receive glucose therapy and were not subjected to fasting before euthanasia and tissue collection, while untreated huR83C, BEAM-301-dosed huR83C, and control mice were in the fed state with ad libitum food access, allowing serum glucose levels to vary based on the time relative to the last food intake.

For the fasting glucose test, BEAM-301-treated huR83C and control mice were transferred into clean cages without food but with free access to water for 24 hours, and blood glucose was analyzed from tail-tip blood at 0 and 24 hours after food deprivation using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.

The body mass index (BMI) value in mice was calculated by dividing the body weight measured in grams by the square of the body length measured in cm, where body length was defined as the distance from the tip of the nose to the base of the tail.

For insulin tolerance testing, 301L-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 4 hours, weighed, and then received an intraperitoneal injection of 0.25 IU/kg of sterile insulin (#I1882; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in PBS.
Blood glucose was measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes after insulin injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System during the insulin tolerance test.
Tissue sections were visualized using the Imager A2m microscope with an Axiocam 506 camera and the ZEN 2.6 software from Carl Zeiss.
Statistical analyses were performed using two-tailed unpaired T tests in the GraphPad Prism Program, version 10.2.2.
Data are presented as Mean values ± SEM, with individual data points for each animal displayed, and significance is denoted by * for p<0.05 and ** for p<0.005.

In the 3-week study, untreated huR83C mice with a 3-weeks survival rate of 39% were included as additional controls.

Blood glucose was measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes after insulin injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.
Permeabilized microsomes were prepared by incubating intact microsomes in sucrose buffer containing 0.2% sodium deoxycholate for 20 minutes on ice.

Phosphohydrolase reaction mixtures of 50 μl containing 50 mM sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 6.5), 2 mM EDTA, 10 mM G6P, and 100–200 μg of permeabilized microsomes were incubated at 30 °C for 10 minutes.

Images of the tissue sections were acquired using an Imager A2m microscope equipped with an Axiocam 506 camera and ZEN 2.6 software from Carl Zeiss.

The study design failed to pre-register the twelve primary outcomes or establish a hierarchical testing strategy, meaning the multiple testing issue originates from the experimental structure rather than the analysis code.

The validity of the False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustment is compromised because the twelve endpoints were selected post-hoc without an a priori primary hierarchy, rendering the multiple-comparison correction cosmetic.

Data was acquired across twelve domains without a pre-specified primary hierarchy, indicating that the lack of experimental structure is a fundamental design failure that cannot be corrected by post-hoc statistical adjustments.

The provided raw data files are missing the pre-registration protocol, the exact random seed, and specific software versions, which prevents verification of whether the results for the two robust outcomes hold under proper constraints.

Determining if the signal magnitude for the two outcomes justifies a new trial requires the exact effect sizes and their 95% confidence intervals, which are currently unavailable to distinguish the statistics from noise.

The study's methodology is compromised by the post-hoc selection of two endpoints from a set of twelve possibilities without pre-registration, a design choice that likely renders any statistical correction insufficient to control the family-wise error rate.

Verification of the results is impossible because the provided materials include raw data but omit the specific code environment, pre-registration protocol, and cleaning steps required to reproduce the analysis.

The study's validity is undermined by an unregistered design that invites alternative explanations, creating a critical gap between the lack of statistical power and the actual biological signal measured.

The study's read filtering pipeline explicitly uses a minimum average quality score threshold of Q>30 and a quantification window of -w 20 -wc-10, which are specific methodological parameters that could independently skew allele frequencies and must be verified for sensitivity before validating confidence intervals.

The 1.5 mg/kg treatment group in the study has a sample size of n=5, a severe methodological limitation that prevents the stabilization of variance in allele frequency quantification and renders the data insufficient for robust statistical validation.

The sample size of n=5 creates a fundamental power problem that makes it impossible to derive a meaningful 95% confidence interval for allele frequencies, requiring an increase to at least n=15 to make claims of stable quantification statistically defensible.

The two outcomes in the study were selected post-hoc from a larger set, and with a sample size of n=5, implementing a correct multiple-testing correction is effectively impossible, resulting in 95% confidence intervals too wide to distinguish true biological effects from random noise.

The study utilized CRISPR gene-editing technology in Drosophila to introduce targeted breaks into the genome alongside a molecular template for repair. The experiments involved multiple genes, template designs, and editing strategies to identify the integration of the repair template molecule at unintended genomic locations.
The study employed CRISPR/Cas9 based genome editing using Homology Directed Repair (HDR) from template vector sequences for Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing.
The researchers observed the deviation from the desired edit at multiple genomic locations, using different HDR vectors and multiple genome editing designs.
To avoid undesired events, the study generated a novel HDR template vector that enables the identification and exclusion of animals with unwanted insertions.

Germline genome editing in Drosophila melanogaster was performed by injecting Drosophila embryos with plasmids expressing guide RNAs and a plasmid containing the edited target sequence flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms. The Drosophila embryos used for the injection expressed germline Cas9 to facilitate the cleavage of the targeted locus.

The HDR template plasmid included an eye expression DsRed selectable cassette to facilitate the identification of animals with successful genome editing. The study utilized a novel and versatile HDR template vector designed to enable single-vector HDR genome editing containing both the template and guide RNA sequences.

The study investigated the frequency of undesired mutagenic insertions of the HDR donor plasmid template vector into the genome during homology-directed repair (HDR) directed genome editing in Drosophila. The authors observed that this vector template insertion occurs at a high frequency with multiple template vectors.

The study utilized two gRNAs designed with CRISPR Optimal Target Finder to create double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 of the Vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) gene in Drosophila. The homology-directed repair donor was a pHSG298 plasmid containing an ALFA epitope tag, an eye DsRed selection cassette, and approximately 1 kb long homology arms.

Fifteen genome-edited Drosophila animals were recovered with eye DsRed expression, and the presence of the ALFA tag was assessed by PCR genotyping using primers specific for the ALFA tag and VGAT flanking regions outside the homology arms. The presence of unwanted pHSG298 vector sequences was tested by PCR amplification using primers specific for the pHSG298 vector, which successfully amplified products from genomic DNA of unwanted editing lines but not from correctly edited lines or controls.

The study used western blotting to analyze homozygous animals from individual lines for the expression of Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43 proteins, identifying 18 of 22 lines where only hTDP-43 was expressed.
The researchers confirmed the editing events in the identified lines using genomic DNA sequencing.

To investigate lines expressing both Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43, the researchers designed a forward primer in the Drosophila TBPH gene and a reverse primer for the hTDP-43 gene to amplify the region between these genes.
Using genomic DNA from Drosophila lines expressing both hTDP-43 and TBPH as a template, the researchers amplified a ~10 kb product and sequenced it to determine the nature of the insertion.
The researchers examined the precise sequence where both the 5' and 3' gRNAs were designed to target to determine the insertion point of the vector sequence.

To determine if the HDR donor vector sequence was present in all incorrectly edited animals, the researchers designed primers to amplify the region between the lac promoter and pUC ori sequence of pCR4.

The researchers found that 100% (4 out of 4) of incorrectly edited animals had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome, while no product could be amplified from the genomic DNA derived from back-ground control or correctly edited animals.

Two guide RNA sequences were designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder software to target regions outside the 3' and 5' UTRs of the Drosophila TBPH gene, specifically targeting the neighboring genes bgcn and cpes to induce Cas9-dependent double-strand breaks.
The guide RNA sequences were synthesized and inserted into the pCFD3 plasmid vector to facilitate expression in germline cells via transgene injection.

A homology-directed repair template plasmid was generated containing approximately 1 kb of 5' and 3' sequences homologous to the Drosophila TBPH genomic region, an artificial replacement exon encoding human hTDP-43, and a DsRed selection cassette, all cloned into the pCR4 plasmid vector.
The guide RNA encoding plasmids and the homology-directed repair replacement cassette were co-injected into Drosophila strains that express Cas9 in the germline.

Genome-edited Drosophila animals were identified by eye-specific expression of DsRed, and the presence of the undesired vector backbone in the genome was detected by genomic DNA PCR using primers specific for the pCR4 vector and the TBPH/hTDP-43 junctions.
The study analyzed 18 Drosophila lines with correctly replaced TBPH genes and 4 lines with incorrect insertion of the template vector backbone to assess the frequency of undesired mutagenic events.

The study utilized two gRNAs targeting exon 12 of the Glutamate Receptor IIA (GluRIIA) gene and a pCR4 HDR vector containing homology arms designed to replace two amino acids, using eye DsRed expression to select editing events. Twelve DsRed expressing Drosophila lines were recovered and analyzed by PCR genomic amplification and sequencing.

DNA sequencing of the eleven incorrectly edited Drosophila lines revealed two peaks in the chromatogram, indicating the presence of both unmutated and modified GluRIIA nucleotides. PCR for pCR4 vector sequences from genomic DNA confirmed that all eleven incorrectly edited lines had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome.

The pCR4 plasmid template contained the mutated GluRIIA exon 12 and a removable DsRed cassette flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms. Genomic DNA PCR amplification using primers specific for pCR4 identified the vector backbone sequence in the incorrectly edited GluRIIA Drosophila lines, but not in the correctly edited line or controls.

The study designed a High-Fidelity Donor (HDR) template cloning vector named pVID (Vector Insertion Detector) to express the ZsGreen1 fluorescent protein under the eye P3 promoter if the vector backbone integrates into the genome. This design incorporated a completely exogenous gene for negative selection to independently identify and exclude vector insertional mutagenic events from the analysis.

For the genome editing of Synapsin, the researchers designed two gRNAs using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder and an HDR donor plasmid containing homology arms, a Synapsin sequence with ALFA epitope tags, and an eye DsRed selection cassette. The pVID vector was employed as the cloning vector for this specific editing procedure.

The study utilized the pVID cloning vector as the backbone for homology-directed repair (HDR) templates, which contained an Ampicillin resistance gene, a Drosophila U6:3 promoter for gRNA expression, a multiple cloning site, and a ZsGreen selection cassette with a 3xP3 eye promoter, ZsGreen fluorescent protein coding sequence, and SV40 terminator.

The CRISPR/Cas9 strategy for Synapsin gene editing employed two guide RNAs to create double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 and after exon 2, using an HDR template that included the desired edit, a DsRed cassette selection flanked by homology arms, and two gRNAs under the control of the dU6:3 promoter.

Researchers performed PCR for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA derived from Drosophila lines to identify undesired vector insertion events, finding that all ZsGreen expressing lines (8 of 8 for Synapsin and 5 of 5 for GluRIIC) had template vector insertion, while DsRed expressing lines without ZsGreen expression showed no evidence of vector template sequences.

A second CRISPR/Cas9 HDR genome editing procedure was conducted using pVID to insert sequences into the GluRIIC gene, which encodes an obligate Glutamate receptor, utilizing an HDR template with the desired insertion and an eye DsRed selection cassette.

The study utilized Drosophila germline genome editing with five fully independent homology directed repair (HDR) procedures, generating an average of 54% (n=71) of edited lines with undesired vector insertion.
Guide RNA (gRNA) sequences were designed using the CRISPR Optimal Target Finder software based on conventional on-target and off-target selection criteria.
The HDR repair templates used a conventional design featuring approximately 1 kb flanking homology arms and included mutated PAM sequences.
The study employed germline Cas9 expressing animals from the stocks nos-cas9 attp2 BL 78782 and nos-cas9 attp40 BL 78781 for the genome editing experiments.

The HDR donor vectors utilized in the study included backbones pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID (ZsGreen), with specific homology arm sizes ranging from 602 bp to 1328 bp and cutting distances from the edit site ranging from 5 bp to 1895 bp.
The study used an eye expression DsRed selection cassette to identify editing events, which allowed for the 'scarless' removal of the marker after successful transgene or genome edit identification.

The study expresses Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells under the nos promoter to enable homology-directed repair (HDR). The authors note that other Cas9 sources, such as different promoters or expression levels, could influence backbone vector insertion, with very high levels of Cas9 being toxic.

The study routinely uses two selection cassettes to improve the efficiency of HDR-mediated genome editing: a positive selection dsRed cassette to indicate an editing event and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to eliminate events where the HDR template vector has inserted into the genome.

The full sequences for the 7ALFA-Synapsin HDR construct were synthesized and cloned into a pVID vector by Genscript.

The GluRIIC HDR construct in pVID targeted the middle of exon 10 and the intronic region between exon 2 and 3, included a Myc tag and an excisable dsRed selection cassette, and was flanked by two 600-700 bp homology arms.

The pVID HDR vector was generated by inserting a Drosophila eye negative selection cassette (3xP3 promoter, ZsGreen fluorescent protein, SV40 terminator) upstream of a dU6:3 gRNA promoter and a multiple cloning site, which was subcloned into pUC57-mini vector by Genscript.

Transgenic Drosophila melanogaster lines were generated by injecting embryos expressing Cas9 under the germ cell specific nos promoter with the HDR construct and gRNA expressing vectors, performed by Genetivision (Stafford, TX, USA) or FlyORF (Zürich, Switzerland).

The methods section does not specify the batch composition of the LNP formulation, creating an uncontrolled variable where lipid component consistency across treatment arms cannot be verified, thereby confounding observed outcomes with non-specific delivery responses.

The methods section fails to specify the lipid-to-RNP mass ratio, a parameter that likely results in the lipid content exceeding the cargo by roughly eight times, thereby diluting the effective concentration and biasing the interpretation of specific editing effects.

The experimental design relied on sample sizes of n=5 per group, which provides negligible statistical power to distinguish true editing effects from batch variability and fails to account for multiple comparisons, meaning any reported significance is likely a false positive driven by uncorrected testing.

The inability to distinguish the 265 μV ERG b-wave rescue from non-specific lipid toxicity is exacerbated by the n=5 per group sample size, which yields negligible statistical power. Without a proper vehicle control and given these tiny sample sizes, the effect is statistically fragile, preventing a claim that the metabolic correction is actually caused by the editor rather than confounders.

The lack of multiple comparison corrections renders the reported p-values statistically meaningless given the number of tests run, and the n=5 per group sample size provides negligible power to distinguish confounders. Consequently, the observed 'rescue' is likely an artifact of batch variability or non-specific lipid toxicity, and the effect size is likely an overestimate rather than a true therapeutic effect.

The study's tiny sample sizes and missing error margins render the data statistically indistinguishable from chance, akin to interpreting a coin flip with only five tosses. This lack of statistical power means the reported improvement cannot be attributed to the medicine rather than side effects of the delivery method, as the error margins are too large to rule out luck.

The off-target screening study lacks critical acquisition parameters, specifically the sequencing depth and library preparation methods, which prevents independent verification of whether the reported insertion sites are genuine biological edits or alignment artifacts.

The therapeutic efficacy claim is methodologically unsupported because the study fails to document the specific physical formulation variables and delivery parameters, leaving the observed benefits unverifiable and potentially attributable to unreproducible experimental conditions rather than the genetic tool itself.

The 300-fold efficiency gain is likely an artifact of the specific SM102 lipid formulation rather than a general property of the gene-editing tool, a conclusion necessitated by the absence of documented synthesis parameters for the delivery vehicle.

The therapeutic effect may be driven entirely by the specific LNP formulation rather than the editor itself, a critical variable that remains undocumented in the current evidence and prevents valid extrapolation to general clinical use.

documents: LNP-encapsulated adenine base editor and prime editor RNPs using the ionizable lipid SM102 resulted in in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold with respect to the delivery of the naked RNP.
The in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements for LNP-encapsulated adenine base editor and prime editor RNPs were observed without detectable off-target edits.
The efficiency of precise repair via homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template is low compared with non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), especially in post-mitotic cells such as neurons.

The DNA-repair mechanisms that enable base and prime editing are cell-cycle independent, allowing high editing efficiencies to be maintained in post-mitotic cell types when genome editing is performed in vivo.

The net size of guide RNA constructs along with base or prime editors exceeds the packaging limits of most commonly used viral vectors, such as lentiviruses and adeno-associated viruses, often requiring the editors to be split into two viral vectors.

Prolonged expression of base and prime editors leads to an increased risk of off-target editing at less-favoured sites on the genome and transcriptome, either in a Cas9-dependent or in an effector-dependent manner.
There is a non-zero risk of viral genome integration, even when non-integrating viral vectors are used, and this risk could be worsened by the deployment of Cas9 nucleases and nickases.

Real-world human data for AAV-mediated delivery of retinal pigment epithelium-specific 65 kDa protein (RPE65) by voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) show that the therapeutic effect may be maintained for 7 years and potentially longer.
Protein expression after subretinal delivery of mRNA was detected within 4 hours and lasted for up to 7 days.
The study utilized a screening of cell-penetrating peptides and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid dissociation constants (pKa) greater than 6.
The study demonstrated the restoration of visual function in a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration using purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticle LNPs.

Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) of ABE and PE proteins was performed relative to standards including blue dextran (2,000 kDa), thyroglobulin (670 kDa), γ-globulin (158 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and vitamin B12 (1.35 kDa).
Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) profiles of ABE with guide RNA in PBS containing 10% (w/v) sucrose were averaged over n=3 replicates.
Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) profiles of PE with guide RNA in PBS were averaged over n=3 replicates.
In the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line, Lipofectamine 3000-delivered Cre recombinase achieved up to 40% color switching, while unmodified Cre recombinase induced up to 4.4% conversion.
TAT-Cre and ANTP-Cre fusions enhanced delivery to up to 28% and 45% respectively, whereas CPP5-Cre did not enhance delivery in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line.
