documents: The study utilized the ionizable lipid SM102 and the synthetic lipid DMG-PEG 2000 to formulate lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) for encapsulating adenine base editor and prime editor ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).
The lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) were produced using microfluidic mixing.
Cell-penetrating peptides were used either covalently fused to the protein or as excipients to enhance the efficiency of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery.
The CRISPR/Cas9 system consists of a Cas9 nuclease targeted by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and a guide RNA that focuses Cas9 binding on a 20-bp-long DNA protospacer.

Base and prime editors fuse a DNA effector domain to a partially inactivated Cas9 domain, termed a Cas9 nickase, to avoid non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and cytotoxicity caused by double-stranded DNA breaks.

The net size of guide RNA constructs along with base or prime editors exceeds the packaging limits of lentiviruses (LV) and adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), often requiring base and prime editors delivered by AAV to be split into two viral vectors.

Transient delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 machinery can be achieved via virus-like particle (VLP) delivery, mRNA lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, or direct ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery as naked RNP or as a lipoplex with cationic lipid reagents such as Lipofectamine 2000.

The study utilized purified adenine base editor (ABE) and prime editor (PE) ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to restore visual function in a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration.
The lipid nanoparticles were formulated using cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid dissociation constants (pKa) greater than 6.
Purification of Cre recombinase was performed using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), with purity assessed via SDS-PAGE and western blot analysis.

ABE and PE proteins were purified using TALON chromatography, 1D4 chromatography, and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), with contaminating nucleic acids monitored by absorbance spectra at 260 nm relative to 280 nm.
Size-exclusion chromatography standards included blue dextran (2,000 kDa), thyroglobulin (670 kDa), γ-globulin (158 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and vitamin B12 (1.35 kDa).
Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) profiles for ABE with guide RNA were measured in PBS containing 10% (w/v) sucrose, while DSF profiles for PE with guide RNA were measured in PBS.
In vitro activity assays for ABE and PE were visualized using urea-PAGE gels imaged for fluorescein and SYBR Gold, with controls including no substrate, substrate-only, no epegRNA, and no dNTP.

The study utilized a fluorescent rd12 reporter cell line created by retrovirally transducing NIH/3T3 cells with a construct containing a fragment of the Rpe65 rd12 complementary (c)DNA with an in-frame nonsense mutation flanked by mCherry and eGFP. Successful base or prime editing of this construct results in the expression of the mCherry-eGFP fusion protein, whereas unedited cells express only mCherry due to the stop codon.

Adenine base editing via plasmid transfection of ABE8e with a previously validated rd12 sgRNA achieved 22% editing efficiency by next-generation sequencing and 32% conversion by flow cytometry in the rd12 reporter cells. The addition of 10% w/v sucrose to the RNP mixture boosted ABE8e delivery, and the non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide further enhanced this delivery by 1.5-fold.

Prime editing (PE) delivery to the rd12 reporter cells showed no activity with 2% sucrose but exhibited activity when delivered with 10% sucrose. The non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide improved the delivery efficiency of the PE2 RNP by approximately 1.6-fold, though overall efficiencies remained low.

The in vivo experiments used the rd12 mouse model of Leber congenital amaurosis, which features a nonsense mutation in Rpe65 that abolishes RPE65 expression and prevents visual chromophore production. The subretinal delivery formulations tested included Cre recombinase delivered alone, with Lipofectamine 3000, with the 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, or fused with CPP5, TAT, or ANTP peptides.

The study utilized three cell-penetrating peptides (TAT, CPP5, and ANTP) fused to the N-terminus of Cre recombinase and ABE8e-SpCas9-NG, and a 1D4 peptide tag fused to the C-terminus of ABE8e and PE2.

Cre recombinase was purified using nickel metal-affinity chromatography (Ni-NTA) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC), while ABE8e was purified using TALON metal and 1D4 affinity columns followed by SEC.
PE2 was purified using 1D4 immunoaffinity followed by an additional heparin chromatography step to maximize separation from impurities.
Size exclusion chromatography effectively removed contaminating nucleic acids and aggregates from ABE8e after immunoaffinity chromatography.
ABE8e ribonucleoprotein (RNP) stability was enhanced by refolding the single guide RNA (sgRNA) through heating and slow cooling, and further stabilized by 10% (w/v) sucrose.

PE2 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) stability was higher than PE2 protein alone, but heat refolding of the engineered prime-editing guide RNA (epegRNA) provided no additional stability benefit, and sucrose was not required for solubility.
All sgRNAs and epegRNAs used in the study were heat refolded for consistency.

The in vitro delivery assay used the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cultured cell line, which expresses green fluorescent protein (GFP) constitutively and uses a stop codon to prevent red fluorescent protein (RFP) expression until Cre-mediated excision occurs.
Lipofectamine 3000 was used as a positive control for delivering Cre recombinase as a lipoplex in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line.
A non-covalent complex of Cre with the CPP peptide 6×His-CM18-PTD4 was used to enhance delivery efficiency.

In vivo activity was evaluated by subretinal injection into ROSA mT/mG mice, which constitutively express membrane-targeted tdTomato and use a polyadenylation stop signal to prevent enhanced GFP (eGFP) expression until Cre-mediated excision.
Primary ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts were isolated and cultured to assess Cre delivery, with Lipofectamine 3000 serving as the positive control for protein delivery.
In vivo positive controls for subretinal injection included AAV1-CMV-Cre and engineered viral-like particles (eVLPs) packaging Cre protein.
The 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide modestly improved the delivery efficiency of PE2 RNP by approximately 1.6-fold, although overall efficiencies remained low.

Subretinal injection of ABE8e RNP rescued the scotopic dark-adapted flash electroretinography (ERG) b-wave in rd12 mice, with the low-NaCl, high-sucrose formulation producing more robust rescue than other formulations.
Genomic DNA and transcripts from RPE samples of treated mice showed up to 2% on-target genomic editing, corresponding to up to 7% on-target base editing in cDNA.
The ABE editing outcomes were distributed approximately equally between precise edits and edits with at least one bystander adenine deaminated.
Purified RNP led to more precise ABE editing than eVLP packaging of the same ABE8e, which resulted in multiple deaminated adenines.
Binding of sgRNA by ABE changes the net charge from a zeta potential of +4.4 mV to -7.6 mV, suggesting efficient capture by cationic lipids.
Delivery of ABE RNP in vitro via a lipoplex with Lipofectamine 3000 was efficient in the rd12 reporter cell line at concentrations as low as 20 nM (4.5 µg ml⁻¹).
The formulation of ABE8e RNP optimal in vitro consisted of 50 pmol (11.2 µg) RNP per µl of Lipofectamine 3000, equating to 5.6 µg RNP per eye.
The in vivo failure of the optimal in vitro formulation to restore ERG responses in rd12 mice may correspond to toxicity from a high dose of Lipofectamine 3000 (50% by volume, 0.5 µl per eye).
Substantially higher rescue was observed when using a 5-fold lower dose of Lipofectamine 3000 with the same amount of ABE RNP.

The ABE RNP formulation required stability at pH 6.0 and in 25% ethanol for LNP encapsulation. The prototypical lipid mixture consisted of ionizable lipid, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol, and 1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000 (DMG-PEG 2000) at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5.

Three specific ionizable lipids with pKa values above 6.0 were used to prevent ABE inactivation: SM102 (pKa 6.68), CL4H6 (pKa 6.25), and DODMA (pKa 6.59). The resulting LNPs exhibited a hydrodynamic diameter between 200 and 250 nm as measured by dynamic light scattering.

Encapsulation of ABE RNP within LNPs was verified by immunoprecipitation using 1D4 resin followed by anti-Cas9 western blot analysis, where ABE RNP LNPs were detected in the non-bound fraction. A control using B6-30 resin directed against the N terminus of rhodopsin confirmed the epitope specificity of the ABE binding.

ABE RNP LNPs delivered active ABE to rd12 reporter cells with high conversion efficiency, reaching nearly 100% for SM102 LNPs. A concentration as low as 20 nM ABE RNP (4.5 µg ml⁻¹) in SM102 LNPs elicited nearly total conversion of the reporter cells.

The rd12 reporter system uses a CMV promoter to express mCherry and eGFP with an intervening Rpe65 rd12 genomic sequence containing a c.130 C > T (p.R44X) mutation that prevents eGFP expression until base editing restores the reading frame. Successful delivery is indicated by the co-expression of mCherry and eGFP.

In vitro delivery assays tested ABE in the presence of 2% (w/v) sucrose, 10% (w/v) sucrose, and 0.5 µM ABE with 10% (w/v) sucrose and 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, where 1 µM ABE corresponds to 224 µg ml⁻¹. In vivo ERG response curves were measured in rd12 mice two weeks post-treatment with ABE RNP in the presence of high and low NaCl and sucrose, with and without 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide.
LNPs formulated with 2.5% 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (SOPS) and SM102 remained stable for at least 28 days at -80 °C and at least 14 days at 4 °C.

The ABE RNP LNP preparation used a concentration of 2 μM (0.45 mg ml⁻¹, 450 ng per eye), which is at least 10-fold lower than the 20-36 μM (4.5-8.1 mg ml⁻¹, 4.5-8.1 μg per eye) concentrations used for RNPs formulated with sucrose or Lipofectamine 3000.
LNPs without DMG-PEG 2000 lipid exhibited the highest particle size and were not active in vitro, indicating that DMG-PEG 2000 is indispensable for RNP encapsulation.
LNPs with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 achieved nearly 100% cell conversion at 5 nM (1.1 μg ml⁻¹) ABE RNP, a concentration 4-fold lower than that required for LNPs with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000.
The optimal formulation for full ABE RNP encapsulation, confirmed by 1D4 immunoassay and size-exclusion chromatography, was a lipid:sgRNA weight ratio of 40:1 with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000.
Cryoelectron microscopy confirmed that the optimized ABE RNP LNPs are intact and uniform particles with an approximate diameter of 100 nm.
Targeted proteomics showed that Cas9 and TadA* deaminase peptides were detected at the same level within the LNPs, indicating the presence of intact, full-length ABE8e protein.
In vivo testing showed that SM102 LNP-RNP with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 resulted in a maximal ERG b-wave rescue of 368 μV, compared to 265 μV for SM102 LNP RNPs with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000.
PE2 RNP delivery in vitro via Lipofectamine 3000 was efficient at 500 nM (149 μg ml⁻¹), a concentration higher than the 20-100 nM (4.5-22.4 μg ml⁻¹) range required for ABE RNP.

Encapsulating PE2 RNP into LNPs with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 resulted in detectable unencapsulated PE2 protein and larger particle sizes, whereas increasing DMG-PEG 2000 to 2.5% eliminated detectable unencapsulated PE2.

Cas9 and the reverse transcriptase (MMLVRT) were not detected at equimolar concentrations within the PE2 RNP LNPs, indicating a gap in LNP formulation or PE2 purification that may require further improvement.
PE2 RNP LNPs achieved an ERG b-wave amplitude rescue exceeding 300 μV in rd12 mice, comparable to the magnitude of rescue achieved by ABE RNP LNPs.

PE2 RNP LNP particle-size distribution parameters are d=270 nm (PdI=0.068) with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipid SM102, d=298 nm (PdI=0.024) with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipid CL4H6, d=176 nm (PdI=0.096) with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipid DODMA, and d=194 nm (PdI=0.040) with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 and ionizable lipid SM102.

The PE2 RNP LNP delivery experiment utilized a concentration of 20 nM, which corresponds to 6 μg ml^-1, and the cryoelectron-microscopy image of the PE2 RNP LNP containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 is presented in Figure 5e.

The ABE RNP LNP formulation used for in vivo delivery contained the ionizable lipid SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000, with an ABE RNP concentration of approximately 2.5 μM and a dose of 560 ng RNP per eye.
The ABE RNP LNP formulation containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 was administered at a concentration of approximately 2.3 μM with a dose of 515 ng RNP per eye.
The ABE RNP LNP formulation containing ionizable lipid DODMA and 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 was administered at a concentration of approximately 1.8 μM with a dose of 403 ng RNP per eye.
In vitro delivery of ABE RNP to rd12 reporter cells was tested at a concentration of 20 nM (4.5 μg ml⁻¹) for incubation periods ranging from 1 to 48 hours.
The LNP size-distribution parameters for the SM102 formulation with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 were a diameter of 228 nm and a polydispersity index of 0.072.
The LNP size-distribution parameters for the CL4H6 formulation with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 were a diameter of 235 nm and a polydispersity index of 0.132.
The LNP size-distribution parameters for the DODMA formulation with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 were a diameter of 249 nm and a polydispersity index of 0.079.
The optimized ABE RNP LNP was injected subretinally into 3-4-week-old juvenile rd12 mice, with physiological assessments performed two weeks after injection.

ABE protein residence time was determined by injecting the optimized ABE RNP LNP subretinally into wild-type mice and sampling at sequential intervals, with ABE detectable up to 24 hours in the neural retina and up to 48 hours in the retinal pigment epithelium.
The in vivo editing efficiency was quantified as 0.30% precise correction of Rpe65 genomic DNA by ABE and 0.12% by PE, and 1.25% precise correction of Rpe65 transcripts by ABE and 1.28% by PE.
Off-target editing was analyzed using supplementary figures, and no editing was detected when ABE and PE RNPs were complexed with guide RNAs that did not target the Rpe65 locus.

The lipid content in the LNP formulation exceeds the weight of the ribonucleoprotein complex by approximately eight times, creating a potential translational challenge for non-human primates or humans.
LNPs with a diameter below 100 nm are more readily internalized by cells, a characteristic that may enhance uptake in the RPE due to its tight junctions and phagocytic role.
Replication is blocked by the lack of experiments correlating functional Rpe65 mRNA levels with the zygosity of corrected Rpe65 alleles in rd12 mice.
Homozygous RPE65-P2A-CreERT2 knock-in mice express RPE65 at levels amounting to only 1-5% of wild-type counterparts, yet exhibit ERG responses nearly indistinguishable from wild-type mice.
The study utilized a PE2 editing strategy without the introduction of a second guide RNA that programmes a nick on the unedited strand, which is distinct from the PE3 strategy.
The authors identified a gap where it is unclear whether adopting the PE3 strategy would improve editing outcomes without unacceptable indel formation.
The study used ABE8e N108Q variants to improve the precision of base editing, as detailed in Extended Data Figs. 2a and 3i-k.
The in vivo experiments involved subretinal injection of ABE RNP LNP into WT mice, with tissue lysates collected at indicated hours post-injection for anti-Cas9 western blot analysis.
Genomic DNA and transcripts were analyzed using next-generation sequencing to document Rpe65-editing outcomes after treatment with ABE RNP LNP or PE RNP LNP.

11-cisretinal levels in whole eyes from dark-adapted untreated rd12 mice, ABE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12 mice, PE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12 mice, and WT mice were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).
RPE flatmounts from rd12 untreated, ABE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12, and WT mice were stained for RPE65 (green) and counterstained with ZO-1 (magenta) and DAPI (blue) with a scale bar of 50 µm.
Scotopic flash ERG a-wave and b-wave amplitudes were measured for rd12 mice to assess functional outcomes.

A fundamental gap in understanding the cellular uptake and processing mechanisms for LNPs and RNPs limits the efficiency of these systems. Clarifying these mechanisms is crucial for enhancing delivery efficiency.

Discrepancies in the delivery efficiencies of Cre, ABE, and PE within the study suggest that optimizing the size of the encapsulated protein, the overall diameter of the LNP, the length of the guide RNA, and the surface charge of the protein are crucial factors for improving delivery efficiency.

The RNP LNPs require additional optimization, including fully quantitative characterization of encapsulation efficiency, before advancing to good manufacturing practice production for non-human-primate and human trials.
Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4(ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (JAX 007676).

Cre recombinase expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21star (DE3) (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown in Terrific Broth (Thermo Fisher, 22711-022) with 50 μg ml⁻¹ kanamycin (Goldbio, K-120-SL25) at 37 °C and 190 r.p.m. until an absorbance at 600 nm of 0.5 was reached, after which Cre recombinase expression was induced with 0.5 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (Goldbio, I2481C25) and incubated at 20 °C for 16 h.

Cre recombinase cell pellets were resuspended in Cre-lysis buffer (50 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 1 M NaCl, 1 cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail tablet (MilliporeSigma, COEDTAF-RO) per 50 ml) and lysed by sonication (125-W pulses, 5 s on/5 s off for 10 min) or French press (3 passes at 15,000 psi), followed by centrifugation at 48,500 g for 15 min.

Cre recombinase purification involved incubating the lysate with 1 ml of Ni-Sepharose High Performance beads (Cytiva, 17526801) for 1 h, washing with 40 ml of Cre-wash buffer (25 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl), and eluting with a 30 ml gradient of Cre-elution buffer (25 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole) on a Tricorn 5/50 column connected to a Bio-Rad DuoFlow system at 0.5 ml min⁻¹.

Pure Cre recombinase fractions were identified by SDS-PAGE and Quick Coomassie staining (Anatrace, GEN-QC-STAIN-1L), concentrated, and subjected to size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva, 28990944) or HiLoad 16/600 Superdex 200 pg (28989335) column using P500G buffer (20 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 20% v/v glycerol) as the mobile phase before storage at -80 °C.

ABE and PE expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21star (DE3) (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown in Terrific Broth with kanamycin until an absorbance at 600 nm of 1.5 was reached, after which ABE and PE expression was induced with 0.8% (w/v) rhamnose (Goldbio, R-105-250) and incubated at 17 °C and 190 r.p.m. for 16-24 h.

Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4 (ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice (JAX 007676) were crossed with BALB/cJ albino mice (JAX 000651) to establish the albino ROSA mT/mG line, while C57BL/6J (JAX 000664) and rd12 (JAX 005379) mouse lines were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and housed at the University of California, Irvine on a normal mouse chow diet and a 12 h/12 h light/dark cycle.

The pTAT-Cre plasmid (Addgene 35619) was used as a base for recombinant plasmids, while pCPP5-Cre and pN-Cre inserts were synthesized by GeneWiz and cloned into pET-28b, and the pANTP-Cre plasmid was generated by replacing the TAT sequence with ANTP between Ncol and Ndel cloning sites.

The ANTP DNA sequence was generated by annealing ANTP-Or_F and ANTP-Or_R primers at a 1:1 molar ratio to a total DNA concentration of 80 μM in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 62.5 mM NaCl, and 10 mM EDTA, using a thermocycler protocol of 2 min at 95 °C followed by gradual cooling to 25 °C for 45 min.

Plasmids were propagated in Escherichia coli NEB-5α cells (New England Biolabs, C2987H), and a positive control Cre eVLP was created by subcloning Cre (Addgene 123133) into pCMV-MMLVgag-3xNES-ABE7.10-NG (Addgene 181753) via USER cloning (NEB).

Genes encoding ABE7.10, ABE8e, and PE2 constructs were subcloned into pRha rhamnose-inducible expression vectors via USER cloning (NEB), and the 1D4 peptide with a preceding tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition site was introduced by PCR site-directed mutagenesis and KLD cloning (NEB, M0554S).

Cell-penetrating peptide sequences were introduced into ABE using PAGE-purified single-strand oligonucleotides (Sigma-Aldrich) annealed at a final concentration of 25 μM in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 5 mM MgCl2 by heating at 95 °C for 5 min and slow cooling.

Assembled duplexes were ligated at a 100-fold excess into protein expression vectors linearized with FastDigest Ndel (Thermo Fisher, FD0584), transformed into NEB-5α cells, and plated onto LB-agar plates containing 25 μg ml−1 kanamycin, with candidate clones identified by colony PCR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing (GeneWiz).
Proteins were expressed at 17 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m. for 16-24 h, and cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C and stored at -80 °C.

Thawed cells from a 1.5-l culture were homogenized with a 40 ml Dounce homogenizer in lysis buffer (100 mM Bis-Tris propane, pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 5 mM TCEP, 1 cOmplete Ultra EDTA-Free protease inhibitor tablet per 40 ml) and lysed by sonication with a Qsonica Q125 sonicator (125 W) with a 1/8-inch microtip at 100% amplitude for a total of 20 min (5 s on, 5 s off).
The lysate was clarified two times at 4 °C by centrifugation at 48,500 g for 10 min, and ABE was captured on a 3-ml TALON metal-affinity resin (Takara Bio, 635502).

The TALON resin was washed with 100 ml of lysis buffer without inhibitors and 10 ml of wash buffer (100 mM Bis-Tris propane, pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM TCEP), and ABE was eluted with wash buffer supplemented with 150 mM imidazole.

ABE was purified by immunoaffinity chromatography using a 1D4 resin (Sepharose CL-4B resin; Cytiva, 17043001) with immobilized 5-10 mg ml⁻¹ 1D4 antibody, packed in a DWK Life Sciences Kimble Kontes FlexColumn.
The 1D4 column was washed with at least 40 ml of wash buffer at 0.5 ml min⁻¹, and ABE was eluted with 1 mg ml⁻¹ 1D4 peptide in wash buffer at ~1 ml h⁻¹.

Pooled ABE fractions were purified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column or a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column, eluted with ABE storage buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol).

Pure ABE was concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters with 30-kDa molecular weight cut-off membranes (Merck, UFC903024), sterilized by passage through 0.22-µm filters, quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm, and snap frozen for storage at -80 °C.

PE was lysed using a single pass through the French press and subsequent sonication for 10 min, and purified using metal affinity and immunoaffinity steps identical to ABE, except the wash buffer contained 400 mM NaCl.

PE was subjected to heparin-affinity chromatography (HiTrap Heparin HP 5 ml; Cytiva, 17040703) at 0.5 ml min⁻¹, equilibrated with wash buffer containing 400 mM NaCl, washed with at least 50 ml of wash buffer, and eluted with a 200-ml NaCl gradient (0.4 M-1.0 M).

Pure PE fractions were purified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column with PE-storage buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5% (v/v) glycerol) as the eluent, then concentrated, filtered, quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm, and snap frozen for storage at -80 °C.

The eluent for purification consisted of pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, and 5% (v/v) glycerol. Purified PE was concentrated, filtered, quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm, distributed into aliquots, and snap frozen for storage at -80 °C.

Protein purity was assessed using SDS-PAGE in hand-cast Tris-glycine-SDS discontinuous gels containing 4% acrylamide in the stacking gel (pH 6.8) and 10% acrylamide in the resolving gel (pH 8.8) with 2.7% crosslinker (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio of 37.5:1; Bio-Rad, 1610158). Samples were mixed with 4x-concentrated Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610747) supplemented with 50 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; MilliporeSigma, D9779), denatured at 70 °C for 10 min, and centrifuged before gel application.

Protein concentration was quantified using UV absorption spectroscopy by measuring absorbance at 280 nm with a Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer. Nucleic acid contamination was monitored by the ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to absorbance at 280 nm, with a ratio <0.60 indicating protein free from nucleic acids and a typical A260/A280 value for purified ABE and PE of 0.55.
Extinction coefficients of the constructs were estimated using the ProtParam tool located at https://web.expasy.org/protparam/.

Synthetic 60-bp-long DNA oligonucleotides (Sigma) labelled with fluorescein on the strand undergoing deamination were annealed at a 1:1 ratio in 10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA by incubation at 95 °C for 5 min and subsequent slow cooling to 20 °C.

End-modified sgRNA and epegRNA were ordered from IDT Technologies with 2'-O-methyl groups on the first three and last three nucleotides, and the first and last three phosphodiester bonds replaced with phosphorothioate bonds. The guide RNAs were dissolved in nuclease-free water at 37 °C for 15 min at 500 r.p.m. in a thermomixer and folded by incubation at ~75 °C for 5 min, followed by slow cooling.

Prepared nucleic acids were quantified using UV absorption spectroscopy by measuring absorbance at 260 nm, where an A260 value of 1.0 corresponded to a DNA concentration of 50 µg ml⁻¹ or an RNA concentration of 40 µg ml⁻¹. DNA was stored at -20 °C and RNA at -80 °C.

HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells (GenTarget, SC018-Bsd), NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, and rd12 reporter cells were maintained in DMEM/F12 medium with GlutaMAX supplement (Thermo Fisher, 10565018) or DMEM with glutamine (Thermo Fisher, 11965092), supplemented with 10% FBS (Genesee Scientific, 25-514H) and 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin (Thermo Fisher, 15140122) in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO₂.

Primary fibroblasts isolated from P0-P3 ROSA mT/mG mice were digested using a 1:1 mixture of 0.25% trypsin without EDTA (Thermo Fisher, 15050065) and 5 U ml⁻¹ dispase (STEMCELL Technologies, 07913) for 1 h at 37 °C, followed by digestion with 0.25% collagenase I (Thermo Fisher, 17018029) in serum-free DMEM/F12 for 1 h at 37 °C.

Primary fibroblasts were washed with DMEM/F12 containing 15% FBS and 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin, filtered through a 70-µm strainer, and passaged every 3-4 days using 0.05% trypsin-EDTA (Thermo Fisher, 25300054).

For protein delivery experiments, cells were seeded 24 h before the experiment to reach 50-70% confluency, with specific cell counts of 100,000, 50,000, and 25,000 per well for CS cell line and NIH/3T3 rd12 cells in 24-, 48-, and 96-well plates, and 50,000, 24,000, and 10,000 per well for rd12 reporter cells and primary fibroblasts.

ABE ribonucleoprotein was assembled by incubating ABE with a 1.5-fold molar excess of sgRNA in a reaction buffer containing 20 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH 7.5), 100 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgSO4, 2 mM DTT, and 5% (v/v) glycerol for 15 minutes at room temperature, with additional 10% (w/v) sucrose used when RNPs were assembled above 4 μM.
The ABE deamination reaction was conducted by diluting ABE to 1 μM in the reaction buffer, preheating at 37 °C, and adding 15 ng of DNA substrate (0.02 μM final) for 10-60 minutes for ABE8e.

The ABE reaction was quenched by adding 30 μl of water preheated to 95 °C and incubating for 2 minutes at 95 °C, followed by treatment with 1 μl of RNase A (20 mg ml-1) and 1 μl of proteinase K (20 mg ml-1) for 15 minutes at room temperature.
DNA products were purified using an Oligo Clean and Concentrator kit (Zymo Research, D4061) and then nicked with 5 units of Endonuclease V (EndoV, NEB) for 2-3 hours at 37 °C.

RNPs were diluted with PBS to 1 μM, SYPRO Orange probe was added to a final concentration of 5×, and samples were aliquoted (10 μl per well) into a 384-well plate (Applied Biosystems, 4483319) sealed with optical foil (Applied Biosystems, 4360954).

For RPE flatmounts, the anterior segment and retina were removed from the posterior eyecup under a dissecting microscope, and four radial cuts were made towards the optic nerve to flatten the eyecup.
Samples were permeabilized and blocked in 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, T8532) with 3% normal goat serum (NGS) in PBS for 30 min.
Samples were incubated with mouse anti-RPE65 antibody (1:100; in house) and rabbit anti-ZO-1 polyclonal antibody (1:100; Invitrogen, 61-7300) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100 and 3% NGS overnight at 4 °C.

After washing three times in PBS for 5 min each, samples were incubated with Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher, A11032) and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100 and 3% NGS for 2 h at room temperature in the dark.

Video files were processed into individual frames using Adobe Premiere Rush programme version 10.0.1 (Adobe Systems) to calculate absolute pupil diameters from recorded images.

Mice were dark adapted for 2 days before eye enucleation, and eyes were homogenized in 1 ml of 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) containing 50% (v/v) methanol (Sigma-Aldrich, 34860-1L-R) and 100 mM hydroxylamine (pH 8.0) (Sigma-Aldrich, 159417-100G).

After a 15-minute incubation at room temperature, 2 ml of 3 M NaCl was added to the homogenized eye sample, and the resulting mixture was extracted twice with 3 ml ethyl acetate (Fisher Scientific, E195-4).

The combined organic phase was dried in vacuo and reconstituted in 250 µl hexane, and 100 µl of the extracted retinoids was separated on a Zorbax Sil normal-phase HPLC column (5 µm, 4.6 mm × 250 mm; Agilent Technologies) connected to an Agilent Infinity 1260 HPLC system with a diode-array detector.

HPLC separation used a mobile phase of 0.6% ethyl acetate in hexane (Fisher Scientific, H302-4) at a flow rate of 1.4 ml/min for 17 minutes, followed by a step increase to 10% ethyl acetate in hexane for an additional 25 minutes.
Retinoids were detected by monitoring absorbances at 325 nm and 360 nm using Agilent ChemStation software.

Mice were dark adapted for 1 week before ERG recording, anaesthetized by isoflurane inhalation, and had pupils dilated with 1% tropicamide ophthalmic solution (Akorn, 17478-102-12) and 10% phenylephrine ophthalmic solution (MWI Animal Health, 054243), followed by hypromellose (Akorn, 9050-1).
ERG recording utilized a Diagnosys Celeris rodent-ERG device with ocular stimulator electrodes on corneas, a subdermal reference electrode between the ears, and a ground electrode in the rear leg.
Eyes were stimulated with a green-light flash stimulus (peak emission 544 nm, bandwidth ~160 nm) of -0.3 log (cd s m^-2) light intensity, with 10 stimuli averaged at a 10 s inter-stimulus interval.
ERG data were analysed with Espion V6 software (Diagnosys), and eyes that received LNP and had no ERG response after treatment were excluded from the RNP LNP optimization study analyses.
Pupillary light reflex (PLR) was characterized in mice (n=5 for each group) using the A2000 computerized pupillometer (Neuroptics) after 6 hours of dark adaptation under isoflurane anaesthesia.
The PLR light profile consisted of four white-light stimuli (1.2 log, 10^1.2 W m^-2) each lasting 500 ms, recorded under scotopic conditions with no background illumination.

Pupil responses were recorded using Active Presenter software (v.9.1.3, Atomi Systems) and decomposed into frames using Adobe Premiere Rush (v.10.0.1, Adobe Systems) for manual verification and calculation of absolute pupil diameters.

The buffer for ABE was 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, and 20% (v/v) glycerol, while the buffer for PE was 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, and 5% (v/v) glycerol, with guide RNA dissolved in water.

The final composition of the buffer for ABE RNP assembly was 2.8 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 140 mM NaCl, 10% (w/v) sucrose, and 5.6% (v/v) glycerol, and for PE RNP assembly was 2.8 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 140 mM NaCl, 10% (w/v) sucrose, and 1.4% (v/v) glycerol.

The ionizable cationic lipids used were CL4H6 (Cayman Chemical, 37279, pKa 6.25), SM102 (Broadpharm, BP-25499, pKa 6.68), or DODMA (Avanti Polar Lipids, 890899, pKa 6.59).

Lipids were dissolved in ethanol and rapidly combined with pre-formed RNP at a volume ratio of 1:3 (ethanol:aqueous) and a total lipid:guide RNA weight ratio of 40:1, which corresponds to an approximate total lipid:protein weight ratio of 7.75:1.

The study's anonymized data and GitHub code repository are available, but the README lacks specific software versions and library dependencies, which blocks the reproduction of the exact numerical outputs reported in Table 2.

The absence of specified Python versions and package dependencies prevents independent verification of whether the confidence intervals in Table 2 are artifacts of specific library updates rather than robust statistical results.

The exact random seed and package versions required to generate the corrected p-values are missing, creating a hard blocker for verifying the FDR threshold application and reproducing the two surviving outcomes.

The specific effect sizes and lower bounds of the 95% confidence intervals for the two surviving outcomes are not provided, preventing a precise assessment of the magnitude of benefit beyond the raw p < 0.05 report.

The study design lacks a pre-registered hierarchical testing strategy or explicit alpha-spending protocol for the twelve primary outcomes, which is a methodological gap that must be documented to understand the multiple testing correction context.
The study utilizes the huR83C humanized mouse model, which carries the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant, to evaluate the efficacy of BEAM-301.
BEAM-301 is defined as a formulation of lipid nanoparticles containing a newly engineered adenine base editor.
The experimental protocol involved monitoring the phenotypic correction of BEAM-301 in huR83C mice over a one-year period.
BEAM-301 corrected approximately 60% of the G6PC1-R83C variant in liver cells of the huR83C mice.
A base correction rate of approximately 10% was identified as the threshold for therapeutic efficacy in the huR83C mouse model.

The humanized knock-in G6PC1-R83C mouse strain (huR83C) was generated by inserting the entire human G6PC1-R83C (G6PC1-c.247C > T) coding sequence into exon 1 of the mouse G6pc gene, which knocked out native mouse G6pc gene expression while placing human G6PC1-R83C expression under the control of the mouse G6pc promoter/enhancer.
The huR83C mice lacked hepatic and renal G6Pase-α activity and manifested a human GSD-Ia pathophysiology similar to global G6pc-deficient (G6pc-/-) mice.
A homology directed repair (HDR) strategy utilized AAV to deliver editing reagents to neonatal G6pc-R83C mice, but the efficacy of HDR-mediated editing in non-dividing cells was low.

A non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) strategy utilized lipid nanoparticles (LNP) to deliver editing DNA oligonucleotides to 2- to 4-week-old G6pc-R83C mice, with success dependent on the efficiency of inserting the editing DNA oligonucleotide in the correct orientation.
The base editor used for G6PC1-R83C correction contains an saCas9 nickase domain and a TadA deaminase domain engineered to maximize target adenine editing and reduce bystander adenine editing.
The guide RNA for the G6PC1-R83C base-editing strategy utilizes an saCas9 'NNGRRT' protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) with the target adenine located at position 16.

BEAM-301 is formulated as a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) co-encapsulating the guide RNA and messenger RNA encoding the base editor, and is administered via systemic tail vein injection at doses ranging from 0.1 to 3.0 mg/kg.
Base-editing efficiency of the G6PC1 alleles in isolated liver slices was analyzed via next-generation sequencing (NGS) at 7 days post-dose.

At a BEAM-301 dose of 1.5 mg/kg in heterozygous mice, 40.3% of sequencing reads encoded wild-type G6Pase-alpha, 5.5% contained the nonsynonymous Y85H bystander edit, 0.3% contained a synonymous bystander edit, and 0.7% exhibited indels.

The pathogenic G6PC1-c.247C > T/p.R83C variant contains a single G>A transition mutation on the complementary strand, which can be targeted by adenine base editors (ABEs) to convert A•T to G•C in genomic DNA.
Messenger RNA encoding the ABE and guide RNA targeting the G6PC1-R83C variant were encapsulated in a LNP formulation referred to as BEAM-301.

Untreated littermates expressed negligible hepatic G6Pase-α activity and exhibited a 3-week survival rate of 39%.
Mammalian G6Pase-α proteins share 87-91% amino acid sequence identity, and the G6pc-R83C variant is pathogenic in mice.

A human cDNA encoding the G6PC1-c.247C > T (G6PC1-R83C) open reading frame was inserted into exon 1 of the mouse G6pc gene at the ATG start codon by Taconic Biosciences, creating a premature STOP codon in the mouse G6pc exon 1 coding sequence.

The newly introduced G6PC1-R83C allele carried an additional p.V332L mutation, and transient expression assays in COS1 cells showed that the phosphohydrolase activity of the G6Pase-α-V332L variant retained 81% of wild-type G6Pase-α activity. ABE mRNA and gRNA targeting G6PC1-R83C were co-encapsulated at a 1:1 weight ratio in LNPs generated by mixing an acidic aqueous RNA solution with an ethanol solution containing a proprietary ionizable lipid, distearoylphosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and a lipid-anchored polyethylene glycol from Avanti Polar Lipids.

LNP formulations were dialyzed overnight at 4 °C against 1× Tris-buffered saline (pH 7.4, Teknova 20228), concentrated using 100,000 Da MWCO Amicon Ultra tubes (UFC910024; Millipore Sigma), and filtered with 0.2-μm filters (4602; Pall Corporation).

Genomic DNA was isolated from frozen mouse liver tissues homogenized in Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline using an Omni Prep Multi-Sample Homogenizer (SKU 06-021; Omni International) and the MagMAX™ DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Kit (A36570; Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Genomic DNA samples were eluted in MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Elution Solution, quantified using a Lunatic UV/Vis plate reader (Unchained Laboratory), and normalized to 20 ng/μL using the same elution solution.

huR83C mice were generated in a mixed C57BL/6/129S4/SvJaeJ background (C57BL-50/129-50) by mating heterozygous huR83C/mR83 mice in 100% C57BL background with wild-type mR83/mR83 mice in 100% 129S4/SvJaeJ background, followed by mating heterozygous progeny in the C57BL-50/129-50 background.

The ABE mRNA was synthesized via in vitro transcription from a template plasmid containing a T7 promoter, 5' UTR, base editor open reading frame, 3' UTR, and 120 polyA tail, using the NEB HiScribe T7 High-Yield RNA synthesis kit (E2040S) with CleanCap AG reagent (N-7113) and complete substitution of N1-methylpseudouridine triphosphate for uridine-5'-O-triphosphate (UTP).

Primary human hepatocytes (F00995-P; BioIVT) were seeded in CP medium (Z99029; BioIVT) onto a collagen type I coated 24-well plate (356408; Corning) at a density of 350,000 cells/well and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2.

Lentiviral transduction was performed using ultra-purified recombinant lentivirus (Lot 220807LVB01; Vector Builder, Inc) packaging a copy of G6PC1 encoding the c.247C>T mutation at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 40.

Cells were transfected using MessengerMAX transfection reagent (LMRNA015; ThermoFisher Scientific) co-formulated with base editor mRNA and gRNA at a 3:1 ratio, and genomic DNA was harvested at 7 days post-transfection.

Genomic DNA samples were normalized to 20 ng/µl using MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Elution Solution. Targeted amplicon sequencing utilized 25-µl PCR reactions with Q5 2× Hot Start Master Mix (New England Biolabs), 0.5 mM gene-specific primers (forward: GGGCATTAAACTCCTTTGGG, reverse: AGTCTCACAGGTTACAGGGA for the genomic site; forward: GGTTCCATCTTCAGAGGAAG, reverse: CAGGGAACTGCTTTATCA for the G6PC1-R83C site), and 2 µl of genomic DNA template.

Barcoded amplicons were generated in 25-µl PCR reactions using Q5 2× Hot Start Master Mix, 0.5 mM barcode primers, and 2 µl of the prior PCR reaction. The final clean libraries were quantified using a Qubit 4 Fluorometer (Q33238; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq Instrument.

On-target G6PC1 alleles are defined as the sum of 10G_12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTATGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3') and 12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTATGGACGCTGTCCAAA-3'). Additional baseedited G6PC1 alleles are defined as the sum of 6G (5'-CCAGTGTGGACACTGTCCAAA-3'), 6G_10G_12G (5'-CCAGTGTGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3'), and 6G_12G (5'-CCAGTGTGGACGCTGTC-CAAA-3') edits.

The NGS data analysis pipeline consists of five steps: 1) Illumina demultiplexing, 2) read trimming and filtering, 3) alignment of all reads to the expected amplicon sequence, 4) generation of alignment statistics and quantification of base-edited alleles, and 5) calculation of the frequencies of corrected G6PC1 alleles.

Primary human hepatocytes from 3 donor livers (BiolVT) were plated on BioCoat Rat Collagen I, 24-well plates (354408; Corning) and treated with BEAM-301 diluted in INVITROGRO CP media (Z990003; BioIVT). At the 1-week terminal timepoint, cells were harvested and genomic DNA was isolated using the Quick-DNA™ MicroPrep Plus Kit (D4074; Zymo Research).

Animal studies were conducted under protocols approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development or the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at University of Massachusetts Medical School and CRADL in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and abided by the ARRIVE guidelines.
Mice were maintained on a standard NIH-31 Open formula mouse/rat sterilizable diet (Envigo) or Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 diet (labdiet) without restrictions.

Mice were housed in a 12-hour light/dark cycle with an ambient temperature controlled within 65-75 °F (18-24 °C) and humidity between 40-60%, and litter sizes were reduced to 6-8 pups to reduce feeding competition.
Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide following the AVMA guidelines for the Euthanasia of Small Laboratory and Wild-Caught Rodents, 2020 Edition.

BEAM-301 was infused into NB huR83C pups via the temporal vein and into 3W huR83C mice via the retro-orbital sinus, with sex-matched mR83 and mR83/huR83C littermates used as controls. Glucose therapy was not provided to BEAM-301-dosed huR83C mice, and the edited mice were not subjected to fasting before euthanasia and tissue collection.

For the fasting glucose test, BEAM-301-treated huR83C and control mice were transferred into clean cages without food but with free access to water for 24 hours. Blood glucose analysis was performed on blood obtained from the tip of the tail at 0 and 24 hours after food deprivation using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System (HemoCue America) according to manufacturer's instructions.

The BMI value in mice was calculated by dividing the body weight measured in grams by the square of the body length measured in cm, where body length was measured as the distance from the tip of the nose to the base of the tail.

For insulin tolerance testing, 301L-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 4 hours, followed by body weight measurement. Each mouse received an intraperitoneal injection of 0.25 IU/kg of sterile insulin (#I1882; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in PBS, with blood glucose measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes after injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.

Genomic DNA was isolated using the Quick-DNA™ MicroPrep Plus Kit (D4074; Zymo Research) following the manufacturer's protocol. The Cas-OFFinder software tool was run on the GRCh38/hg38 human reference genome using the protospacer sequence and a relaxed PAM requirement (NNGRRN) to identify potential off-target sites.

Off-target sites were enumerated if they matched the input pattern with either 7 or fewer mismatches in the targeted DNA with no bulges, or a DNA or RNA bulge of 2 bases with up to 3 mismatches. A SurePrint Oligonucleotide Library (G7239A; Agilent) containing 14,509 sites was constructed based on these mismatch parameters and genomic annotation.

The ONE-seq assay was performed on the SurePrint Oligonucleotide Library using a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein. Digenome-seq was performed using human genomic DNA isolated from the GM11468 human B-lymphocyte cell line, which is heterozygous for the G6PC1 c.247C > T allele (Coriell Institute, Camden, NJ), and a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

rhAmpSeq panels were constructed to include sites nominated from ONE-seq and Digenome-seq, in silico identified low-mismatch sites, the 1 on-target site, and 20 negative control sites. Genomic DNA was isolated from primary human hepatocytes treated with BEAM-301 at a concentration at or above the EC90 of on-target editing, and multiplex amplicon sequencing via rhAmpSeq (Integrated DNA Technologies) was performed.

The EC90 was measured in primary human hepatocytes that harbor the target site introduced via lentiviral transduction, as healthy human hepatocytes do not harbor the target allele. rhAmpSeq was also performed on untreated, donor-matched primary human hepatocytes as controls.

Sequencing reads were trimmed, stitched, aligned to the GRCh38/hg38 human genome reference sequence, and filtered for a minimum base-quality score of 30 and mapping quality of 10. An odds ratio quantifying the enrichment of each observed variant in the treated sample relative to the untreated sample was calculated, and a Fisher's exact test was used to assess statistical significance based on an empirically determined threshold.

Tissue sections were visualized using the Imager A2m microscope with the Axiocam 506 camera and the ZEN 2.6 software from Carl Zeiss. Statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism Program, version 10.2.2, with two-tailed unpaired T tests.

In the shorter 3-week study, untreated huR83C mice with a 3-week survival rate of 39% were also included as controls.

Permeabilized microsomes were prepared by incubating intact microsomes in sucrose buffer containing 0.2% sodium deoxycholate for 20 minutes on ice.
Phosphohydrolase reaction mixtures (50 µl) contained 50 mM sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 6.5), 2 mM EDTA, 10 mM G6P, and 100–200 µg of permeabilized microsomes, incubated at 30 °C for 10 minutes.
Non-specific phosphatase background was estimated by pre-incubating permeabilized microsomes in 20 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) for 10 minutes at 37 °C to inactivate acid-labile G6Pase-α.

The raw data files are provided, but the pre-registration protocol, exact random seed, and software versions are missing, which blocks verification of whether the two reported outcomes hold under proper constraints.

The twelve endpoints were not pre-registered, and the data was acquired across these domains without a pre-specified primary hierarchy, creating a fundamental lack of experimental structure that invalidates post-hoc statistical adjustments.

The study lacks 95% confidence intervals and precise effect sizes for the two reported outcomes, which prevents distinguishing a meaningful biological signal from random variation and blocks any causal replication.

Replication is blocked by the absence of the code environment, the pre-registration protocol, and the specific cleaning steps, leaving only raw data and a list of two outcomes without the necessary pipeline to verify if results are artifacts of filtering.

The methods section fails to specify the minimum quality score threshold (e.g., Q>30) or the exact window parameters (e.g., -w 20) used during read filtering, making it impossible to verify if the reported allele frequencies are biologically real or artifacts of arbitrary data cleaning.

The study lacks pre-registration, which is a critical gap that prevents the current acquisition parameters from being treated as definitive proof of efficacy, limiting the data's utility to hypothesis generation rather than robust causal validation.

The 1.5 mg/kg treatment group has a sample size of n=5, which is insufficient to stabilize variance in allele frequency quantification, making the current data inadequate for robust statistical validation regardless of script reproducibility.

A sample size of n=5 creates a fundamental power problem where the standard error on allele frequencies is too large to derive meaningful 95% confidence intervals, requiring a minimum of n=15 to make statistical claims of stable quantification defensible.

The selection of two outcomes post-hoc from a larger set, combined with a sample size of n=5, makes correct implementation of multiple-testing correction impossible, rendering any resulting 95% confidence intervals too wide to distinguish biological effects from noise.

The study describes an undesired event in Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing where the template vector employed for Homology Directed Repair (HDR) unwantedly inserts into the genome. This deviation was observed at multiple genomic locations, using different HDR vectors, and across multiple genome editing designs.
The authors generated a novel HDR template vector specifically designed to enable the identification and exclusion of animals containing these undesired vector template genomic insertions.

The full citation for the study is Källstig E, Ruchti E, Raman M, Asadzadeh J, Schneider BL, McCabe BD (2026) Highly frequent undesired insertional mutagenesis during Drosophila genome editing. PLoS Genet 22(7): e1012192. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1012192.
All relevant data for the study on HDR based genome edited animals is available within the manuscript and Supporting Information files.

The research was supported by Swiss National Science Foundation grant numbers CRSII3_154455, 31003A_179587, and 320030-232324, European Union Horizon 2020 Marie Skłodowska Curie grant agreement No 721802, and European Union Horizon 2020 Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement No 945363.

The CRISPR/Cas9 HDR strategy in Drosophila utilizes a template plasmid containing homology arms approximately 1 kb long flanking the edited sequence, along with an eye expression DsRed selectable cassette for identification.

The experimental protocol involves injecting Drosophila embryos with plasmids expressing two guide RNAs and a plasmid containing the edited target sequence, using germline Cas9 expressed via transgenic animals or transient plasmid expression.
18 out of 22 generated Drosophila lines expressed only human hTDP-43 with undetectable Drosophila TBPH, confirmed by western blotting and genomic DNA sequencing of the expected editing event.

4 out of 22 Drosophila lines (18%) expressed both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43, and 100% of these incorrectly edited animals had the entire pCR4 HDR editing template plasmid vector inserted into their genome proximal to the TBPH gene.

The pCR4 vector insertion occurred at the site where a double-strand break was designed to be induced by one of the gRNAs, with the PAM sequence on both sides of the insertion modified to match the edited PAM sequence of the template donor plasmid.
The undesired pCR4 template vector insertion was stably inherited across multiple generations in Drosophila, consistent with germline genome insertion.

The HDR template plasmid contains approximately 1 kb of 5' and 3' sequences homologous to the Drosophila TBPH genomic region, an artificial replacement exon encoding hTDP-43, and a DsRed selection cassette cloned into the pCR4 vector.
Two gRNAs targeting the TBPH 3' and 5' UTR regions were synthesized and inserted into the pCFD3 vector to facilitate Cas9-dependent expression in germline cells.
The gRNA encoding plasmids and the HDR replacement cassette were injected into Drosophila strains expressing Cas9 in the germline, with successfully edited animals identified by DsRed eye expression.

Incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila lines exhibit a genomic insertion of the entire HDR template vector sequence flanked by sequences matching homology arm 2, detectable by a ~10 kb PCR product using a forward primer in the TBPH 3' end and a reverse primer in the hTDP-43 5' end.

The presence of the undesired pCR4 vector backbone in the genome is confirmed by genomic DNA amplification using primers specific for the template pCR4 vector, which are present in vector DNA and incorrectly edited lines but absent in correctly edited lines or controls.
The HDR donor plasmid pHSG298 contained homology arms, the VGAT sequence including an ALFA epitope tag, and an eye DsRed selection cassette, with gRNAs designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder.
PCR genotyping used primers specific for the ALFA tag and VGAT flanking regions outside the HDR homology arms to confirm the ALFA tag insertion in all 15 recovered Drosophila lines.
Ten of the fifteen edited Drosophila lines (66.6%) showed incorporation of pHSG298 vector sequences into the genome, while five lines (33.3%) showed no evidence of donor vector insertional events.

The CRISPR/Cas9 plus HDR strategy targeted two double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 of the VGAT gene using two gRNAs, with the pHSG298 vector providing a template containing an ALFA tag and a removable DsRed cassette flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms.

Agarose gel analysis of PCR products amplified using primers specific for the pHSG298 vector confirmed the presence of pHSG298 sequences in genomic DNA from unwanted editing lines but not in correctly edited VGAT Drosophila lines or controls.

The pVID vector is designed to express the ZsGreen1 fluorescent protein under the eye P3 promoter only if the vector backbone integrates into the genome, serving as a negative selection marker to detect vector insertion events.

The genome editing of Synapsin utilized two gRNAs designed with CRISPR Optimal Target Finder and an HDR donor plasmid containing homology arms, a Synapsin sequence with ALFA epitope tags, and an eye DsRed selection cassette, with pVID serving as the cloning vector.
The HDR template vector for GluRIIA editing was a pCR4 plasmid containing the mutated GluRIIA exon 12, a removable DsRed cassette, and approximately 1 kb long homology arms.
Two gRNAs were designed to target exon 12 of the Glutamate Receptor IIA (GluRIIA) gene to enable double-strand breaks for the HDR editing strategy.

PCR amplification and sequencing of genomic DNA from 12 DsRed expressing Drosophila lines revealed that only 1 line had the correct edit, while 11 lines with incorrect edits contained both unmutated GluRIIA nucleotides and the desired modified nucleotides.
PCR for pCR4 vector sequences from genomic DNA confirmed that all 11 incorrectly edited Drosophila lines had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome.
The study utilized Drosophila germline genome editing with gRNA sequences designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder based on conventional on-target and off-target selection criteria.
The HDR repair templates used in the study featured conventional designs with approximately 1 kb flanking homology arms, the sequence to be inserted or edited, and mutated PAM sequences.

The pVID vector includes an eye expression DsRed selection cassette which allows for the 'scarless' removal of the marker after successful transgene or genome edit identification.
The authors use a positive selection dsRed cassette and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to identify and eliminate events where the HDR template vector has inserted into the genome.
Cas9 is expressed in Drosophila germ cells under the nos promoter to enable HDR, with the note that very high levels of Cas9 can be toxic.
The precise sequence of the HDR vector does not influence genome integration, as insertion was observed with pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID vectors.

The GluRIIC HDR construct included two gRNAs with their respective scaffold sequences interspaced by a tRNA sequence upstream of the edit, and the full sequences were synthesized and cloned in a pVID vector by Genscript.

The pVID HDR vector contains a Drosophila eye negative selection cassette composed of a 3xP3 promoter, a ZsGreen fluorescent protein, and a SV40 terminator inserted upstream of a dU6:3 gRNA promoter, with a multiple cloning site downstream for gRNA and HDR template insertion.

The study lacks a vehicle control group receiving lipid nanoparticles without the editing cargo, which prevents the isolation of specific base editing effects from non-specific delivery responses and blocks causal attribution to the base editor.

The batch composition of the LNP formulation is unspecified, creating a gap that prevents verification of lipid component consistency across the five treatment mice and confounds observed outcomes with non-specific delivery responses.

The methods section fails to document the specific ionizable lipid composition or transfection reagent, which prevents benchmarking against established protocols like those using SM102 and blocks determination of whether outcomes are due to a unique formulation or standard practice.

The methods section leaves the lipid-to-RNP mass ratio unspecified, a critical gap that prevents replicationists from determining the effective concentration of the cargo relative to the carrier load, which likely exceeds the cargo by roughly eight times.

The experiments relied on a sample size of n=5 per group without a pre-specified hierarchy or correction for multiple comparisons, resulting in negligible statistical power that prevents distinguishing true editing effects from the background noise of the delivery system.

The absence of a vehicle control using the identical lipid formulation blocks verification of the therapeutic effect, as it is impossible to distinguish the metabolic changes caused by the genetic modification from non-specific carrier toxicity or physical delivery noise.

The study utilizes n=5 per group, a sample size that yields negligible statistical power to distinguish the 265 μV ERG b-wave rescue from non-specific lipid toxicity or batch variability, thereby blocking the verification of the effect's magnitude.

The lack of multiple comparison corrections renders the reported p-values statistically meaningless, which prevents a valid assessment of whether the observed 'rescue' is a true therapeutic effect or an artifact of the testing procedure.

Independent replication of the off-target screening is currently blocked by the absence of raw FASTQ files, documented sequencing depth, library preparation parameters, and exact software versions for alignment, which are required to distinguish true variants from alignment artifacts or low-coverage noise.

The reported off-target insertion sites lack statistical validity for independent verification because the study omits global false discovery rate corrections for the multiple-testing burden of whole-genome screening, leaving it impossible to determine if the specific p-values represent significant edits or background noise.

The efficacy of the treatment remains unproven for independent replication because the specific physical formulation conditions and documented recipe for the delivery vehicle are missing, meaning results may depend on undocumented variables rather than the genetic tool alone.

A standardized framework for distinguishing clinically relevant off-target events from background noise is missing because the studies fail to explicitly parse complex multi-base variants from beneficial single-base corrections, preventing adequate characterization of the editing outcomes.

The 300-fold efficiency gain is likely an artifact of the specific SM102 lipid formulation rather than a general property of the editor, making it impossible to generalize the results to other clinical scenarios without verifying the delivery mechanism.

The LNP synthesis details constitute the first missing block preventing replication, and without a controlled comparison using identical editors and different lipid formulations plus raw data, the results cannot be verified beyond being a quirk of one specific recipe.

Felgner ${ }^{(1)}{ }^{4} \&$ Krzysztof Palczewski ${ }^{(1)}{ }^{1,3,16,17}$ Delivering ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) for in vivo genome editing is safer than using viruses encoding for Cas9 and its respective guide RNA. However, transient RNP activity does not typically lead to optimal editing outcomes. Here we show that the efficiency of delivering RNPs can be enhanced by cell-penetrating peptides (covalently fused to the protein or as excipients) and that lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating RNPs can be optimized for enhanced RNP stability, delivery efficiency and editing potency. Specifically, after screening for suitable ionizable cationic lipids and by optimizing the concentration of the synthetic lipid DMG-PEG 2000, we show that the encapsulation, via microfluidic mixing, of adenine base editor and prime editor RNPs within LNPs using the ionizable lipid SM102 can result in in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold (with respect to the delivery of the naked RNP) without detectable off-target edits. We believe that chemically defined LNP formulations optimized for RNP-encapsulation stability and delivery efficiency will lead to safer genome editing.

Monogenic diseases arise from genetic mutations that lead to aberrant or absent gene expression, and many lack appropriate therapies. Advances in molecular biology have enabled several treatment approaches to address this unmet medical need and correct the molecular basis of inherited diseases. Gene augmentation therapy, for example, delivers a wild-type (WT) copy of a mutated gene via a viral vector to supplement expression ${ }^{1}$. However, gene augmentation is limited by several major shortcomings, including potential loss of expression over long periods, lack of endogenous gene regulation, the inability to package large transgenes ${ }^{2}$ and low efficacy when treating mutations that act in a dominant manner ${ }^{3,4}$. An alternative approach to gene augmentation is genome editing. By correcting the genomic mutation in situ, a one-time treatment could be curative for the lifetime of the patient ${ }^{5,6}$. Of the gene editing techniques, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) editing has shown great promise and has advanced to clinical trials ${ }^{7}$. While these early trials have focused on treating monogenic diseases, it is possible to envision the application of genome editing for the
treatment or prevention of common diseases with multifactorial or polygenic causes, such as malignancies ${ }^{8,9}$, cardiovascular disorders ${ }^{10}$ or neurodegenerative diseases ${ }^{11}$.

The CRISPR/Cas9 system used in gene editing trials consists of a Cas9 nuclease that is targeted to a genomic site by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and guide RNA that focuses the binding of Cas9 on a 20-bp-long DNA protospacer ${ }^{12}$. While CRISPR/ Cas9 is easily programmed by the substitution of the guide RNA, the double-stranded DNA cleavage mediated by the nuclease can lead to a heterogeneous pool of editing outcomes, namely random insertions and deletions (indels) by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), as well as cytotoxicity, p53 pathway activation, and large chromosomal irregularities and rearrangements ${ }^{7}$.Moreover, the efficiency of precise repair via homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template is low compared with NHEJ, especially in post-mitotic cells ${ }^{13}$, including major cell types of interest such as neurons.

of precise repair via homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template is low compared with NHEJ, especially in post-mitotic cells ${ }^{13}$, including major cell types of interest such as neurons. Two alternatives to genome editing with CRISPR/Cas9 nucleases are base and prime editors, which fuse a DNA effector domain to a partially inactivated Cas9 domain, termed a Cas9 nickase ${ }^{14-16}$. These modifications combine the ease of programmability of CRISPR/Cas9 with the precision and direct chemistry of the effector domain of the base or prime editor, while avoiding NHEJ and cytotoxicity caused by double-stranded DNA breaks ${ }^{17}$. Thus, the purity of editing outcomes is much greater for base and prime editors; because the DNA-repair mechanisms that enable base and prime editing are cell-cycle independent, the high editing efficiencies are maintained in post-mitotic cell types when genome editing is performed in vivo ${ }^{18}$. CRISPR/Cas9 strategies, and base and prime editing in particular, are suitable approaches for dominant-negative diseases through correction of the pathogenic allele ${ }^{19,20}$. However, bystander editing by base editors is a concern ${ }^{21}$, as it could lead to unintended changes and hamper the therapeutic efficacy for the patient ${ }^{21}$. As well, the potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored and documented.

As well, the potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored and documented. One major hurdle that limits the application of base and prime editors is appropriate and efficient delivery of these editing constructs. The current standard for delivery of gene therapy and gene editing constructs is via viral vectors. However, the net size of the guide RNA constructs along with the base or prime editors exceeds the packaging limits of most commonly used viral vectors, such as lentiviruses (LV) and adeno-associated viruses (AAVs); indeed, base and prime editors delivered by AAV often are split into two viral vectors ${ }^{22}$. In addition, while these viral vectors have been engineered to be less immunogenic than their native counterparts, they still express base and prime editors over a sustained period ${ }^{23}$. Whereas the intended 'on-target' site is favoured thermodynamically to be edited, prolonged expression of base and prime editors leads to an increased risk of off-target editing at less-favoured sites on the genome and transcriptome ${ }^{24}$, either in a Cas9-dependent ${ }^{25}$ or in an effector-dependent manner ${ }^{26,27}$. Prolonged exposure to base editors has been also shown to increase bystander editing ${ }^{28}$. Lastly, there is a non-zero risk of viral genome integration, even when non-integrating viral vectors are used ${ }^{29}$, and this risk could even be worsened by the deployment of Cas9 nucleases and nickases ${ }^{30,31}$. Thus, as sustained expression of CRISPR/Cas9 is unnecessary and only risks unintended editing outcomes, CRISPR/ Cas9 should be delivered in a transient manner and rapidly degraded thereafter. Multiple ways of achieving this transient action have been proposed, such as by virus-like particle (VLP) delivery ${ }^{28,32,33}$, mRNA lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) delivery ${ }^{34}$ and by direct ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, either as naked RNP or as a lipoplex with cationic lipid reagents such as Lipofectamine $2000{ }^{35-38}$. Such a variety of approaches has the potential to fine-tune the duration of activity of CRISPR/Cas9 machinery; however, these alternative delivery mechanisms require further refinement.

Conceptually, delivery of preassembled RNPs offers the most rapid onset and the shortest duration of genome editor activity in the cell. Real-world human data for AAV-mediated delivery of retinal pigment epithelium-specific 65 kDa protein (RPE65) by voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) show that the therapeutic effect may be maintained for 7 years and potentially longer, demonstrating sustained expression of the transgene delivered by AAV ${ }^{39}$. Protein expression after subretinal delivery of mRNA was detected within 4 h and lasted for up to 7 days ${ }^{40}$. In the case of RNP, the purified protein is complexed with synthetic guide RNA before direct delivery into cells, thus bypassing the requirement of transcription (AAV, LV) and translation (AAV, LV, mRNA). VLPs that have RNP encapsulated in a viral shell offer the same advantageous activity kinetics as RNP; however, they are not chemically defined, which may complicate their manufacturing and clinical application. Use of purified RNP thus offers the most transient and chemically defined delivery modality for CRISPR/Cas9.

Previously, we reported the successful correction of the causative mutation in the rd12 mouse model of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) through delivery of an adenine base editor (ABE) via $\mathrm{LV}^{41}, \mathrm{AAV}^{42}$ and engineered virus-like particles (eVLP) ${ }^{28}$. Likewise, we recently delivered prime editor (PE) via eVLP and achieved effective and precise correction of the rd12 mutation ${ }^{43}$. However, we expect that we can create a more defined, clinically relevant formulation of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editor through optimization of direct delivery of base- and prime-editor RNPs. Here, following a screening of cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid disassociation constants $\left(\mathrm{p} K_{\mathrm{a}}\right)>6$, we show the restoration of visual function in a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration using purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticle LNPs. The potential for therapeutic benefit from administered proteins hinges upon successful delivery across cellular membranes. A number of agents have been demonstrated to enhance intracellular delivery of genome-editing proteins and RNPs, including CPPs. Accordingly, we genetically fused three different CPPs (TAT, CPP5 and ANTP) ${ }^{44-47}$ to the N terminus of Cre recombinase and ABE8e-SpCas9-NG (hereafter referred to as ABE8e), which recognizes the NG PAM (Fig.1a). To facilitate purification, we also fused the 1D4 peptide tag ${ }^{48}$ to the C terminus of ABE8e and the prime editor protein, PE2 (Fig. 1a). Although Cre recombinase and Cas9-based genome-editing proteins possess distinct physicochemical properties, such as size and charge, we hypothesized that insights from the study of intracellular delivery of Cre recombinase would inform the design of delivery vehicles for ABE8e and PE2.

We first purified Cre recombinase to homogeneity, with or without the N-terminal CPP fusion, through nickel metal-affinity chromatography (Ni-NTA) chromatography (Fig. 1b) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC, Fig. 1c), and confirmed the purity of the product through sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) visualized with Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB) (Fig.1d) and anti-Cre western blot (Fig. 1e). ABE8e was similarly purified through affinity chromatography on TALON metal (Fig. 1e) and 1D4 (Fig. 1f) affinity columns and completed with SEC (Fig. 1g); purity was again assessed by SDS-PAGE with CBB staining and anti-Cas9 western blot (Fig. 1h,i). PE2 was purified in a similar manner as ABE8e, with an additional heparin chromatography step after 1D4 immunoaffinity to maximize separation from impurities (Fig. 1j). We noted that ABE8e after immunoaffinity chromatography still contained contaminating nucleic acids and aggregates; these contaminants were removed effectively by SEC (Fig. 1k). We also noted that ABE8e RNP was more stable than ABE8e protein alone, as determined by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), especially when the single guide RNA (sgRNA) was refolded by heating and slow cooling (Fig. 1l and Supplementary Fig. 1a-f). The ABE RNP was further stabilized by 10\% (w/v) sucrose. Similar to ABE8e, the PE2 RNP complex with an engineered prime-editing guide RNA (epegRNA) was more stable than PE2 protein alone; however, heat refolding of epegRNA had no additional effect on PE2 RNP stability (Fig. 1m and Supplementary Fig. 1g,h). PE RNP did not require sucrose to remain soluble. For consistency, we heat refolded all sgRNAs and epegRNAs used throughout the study. We also assessed the enzymatic activity of our ABE8e and PE2 RNPs through in vitro activity assays to ensure our proteins maintained activity following purification. ABE8e RNP displayed high levels of activity as assessed by an in vitro deamination assay (Fig. 1n,o), and PE2 RNP similarly displayed high levels of activity as assessed by an in vitro reverse-transcriptase extension assay (Fig.1p,q).

CPPs enable efficient delivery of Cre in vitro and in vivo. We first assessed the delivery of Cre recombinase into the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cultured cell line (colour switching, 'CS') for a rapid and convenient fluorescent readout of intracellular protein delivery. The CS reporter cell line expresses green fluorescent protein (GFP) constitutively, while a stop codon upstream of red fluorescent protein (RFP) gene prevents its expression. Upon delivery of Cre, floxed GFP-STOP is excised, enabling RFP expression in place of GFP (Fig. 2a). As a positive control, we delivered Cre recombinase as a lipoplex with Lipofectamine 3000 to confirm the specificity of this cell line, reaching up to 40\% conversion of the cells (Fig. 2b). Cre recombinase alone induced low but detectable (up to 4.4\%) colour switching from GFP to RFP, indicating an ability of unmodified Cre recombinase to cross cell membranes (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). TAT- and ANTP-CPPs resulted in enhancement of Cre delivery (up to 28\% and 45\%, respectively), while the CPP5-CPP did not (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). We also delivered Cre as a non-covalent complex with CPP peptide 6×His-CM18-PTD4 (ref. 49), which increased the delivery of Cre to ~6\% and synergistically enhanced the delivery efficiency of CPP-fused Cre proteins (Fig. 2b,d, and Supplementary Figs. 3a,b and 4a,b). Next, we delivered Cre into ROSA mT/mG mice, a global fluorescent reporter strain for monitoring Cre recombinase activity ${ }^{50}$. All cells from the ROSA mT/mG mouse constitutively express membrane-targeted tdTomato from the Rosa26 locus, while a polyadenylation stop signal prevents the expression of enhanced GFP (eGFP). When Cre recombinase is introduced to the cells, the tdTomato and stop signals are excised, enabling eGFP expression (Fig. 2e). We isolated and cultured primary ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts and demonstrated that Cre recombinase delivered alone resulted in low tdTomato to eGFP conversion, while Cre protein delivered by Lipofectamine 3000 resulted in higher conversion (Fig. 2f,g). In contrast to the results with the CS line, only the fused ANTP peptide modestly improved delivery of Cre recombinase to the ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts (Fig. 2f,g). Consistent with our in vitro findings, Cre recombinase delivered subretinally with Lipofectamine 3000, the 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, or fused CPPs, effected ample eGFP expression in the RPE and photoreceptors (Fig. 21-p). Notably, although not effective in vitro, CPP5-fusion peptide enabled delivery of Cre into the photoreceptors in vivo (Fig. 2n). ## CPPs are unable to efficiently deliver ABE and PE in vitro and in vivo

tably, although not effective in vitro, CPP5-fusion peptide enabled delivery of Cre into the photoreceptors in vivo (Fig. 2n). ## CPPs are unable to efficiently deliver ABE and PE in vitro and in vivo As all of the CPPs were effective to some degree in delivering Cre recombinase in vitro and in vivo, we then applied them for the delivery of ABE and PE to the rd12 mouse model of Leber congenital amaurosis. In these mice, a nonsense mutation in Rpe65 abolishes RPE65 expression ${ }^{41,42}$, leading to a lack of visual chromophore production and photoreceptor light detection; however, successful base or prime editing rescues this phenotype. To enable efficient in vitro screening, we developed a fluorescent rd12 reporter cell line. We retrovirally transduced NIH/3T3 cells with a construct containing a fragment of the Rpe65 rd12 complementary (c)DNA encompassing an in-frame nonsense mutation, which is flanked by mCherry and eGFP. In unedited cells, the stop codon only permits mCherry protein expression and successful transition by base or prime editing results in the expression of the mCherry-eGFP fusion protein (Fig. 3a). We verified that adenine base editing via plasmid transfection of ABE8e with a previously validated rd12 sgRNA ${ }^{42}$ successfully edited the reporter construct and restored eGFP expression, as quantified by next-generation sequencing (22\%, Fig. 3b) and flow cytometry (32\%, Fig. 3c). Unmodified ABE applied on the rd12 reporter cells caused low but detectable conversion of the fluorescent reporter (Fig. 3c,d), but in contrast to fusion with Cre recombinase, the fused CPP peptides did not enhance the delivery of ABE in vitro (Fig. 3d). However, as we previously observed that sucrose promoted stability of the RNP complex (Supplementary Fig. 1c-f), the addition of sucrose (10\% w/v) to the RNP mixture boosted delivery of the ABE8e RNP (Fig. 3d). This was further enhanced 1.5-fold by the addition of the non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, but fused CPPs still did not result in improved delivery efficiency (Fig. 3d).
